subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE ADDITIONAL AID TO CO-OPERATIVE HOUSING
speechtext:

They feel, in this International Year of the Homeless, that this Government's definition of essential needs is preventing hundreds of thousands of Canadians living below the poverty line from receiving government housing assistance.

That this House condemns the Government for creating a state of confusion within its immigration program and for its lack of leadership and vision, which has seriously undermined the confidence of Canadians in the over-all direction of immigration policy;
That this House also deplores the Government's failure to address the growing frustration experienced by large numbers of Canadians who are unable to sponsor successfully family members as immigrants from abroad and its recent actions that undercut Canada's humanitarian assistance and protection for refugees legitimately seeking haven in Canada;
That, therefore, this House urges the Government to:
(1)	recognize the long-standing importance of family class reunification and to re-establish this program as the cornerstone of Canada's immigration;
(2)	adopt a fair, humane and efficient refugee policy which would reinforce Canada's past proud tradition and honour Canada's international obligations under the United Nations Convention relating to the status of refugees, signed in 1951;
(3)	introduce immediately a new and independent refugee determination system that would assure claimants processing that is fair, effective and expeditious while discouraging fraudulent applications; and
(4)	initiate a comprehensive educational program that will fully inform all Canadians of the facts about and benefits resulting from immigration and develop a long-term vision that would utilize immigration as a vehicle to strengthen our national unity and to contribute to greater economic prosperity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Canada has a long-standing history of providing an opportunity for immigrants to start a new life. Past Liberal Governments have been especially hospitable to family reunification and compassionate toward the plight of legitimate refugees. We are a nation which opened its doors to the world and invited people to join in the building of a new country, a new life, and a fresh beginning.
Supply
Immigration has enjoyed a prominent place in Canada's history, but I am troubled by the questionable and confusing actions of the Conservative Government in Ottawa in respect of immigration policy. Thus, we in the Liberal Party have moved the motion today with the hope that by examining the status of our immigration program, the Government will end the uncertainty and aggressive ideology paralyzing the direction of the immigration policy in the country.
For my part, I would like to focus on three issues: family reunification, refugees and the need for a comprehensive vision of immigration. As a Member of Parliament for the riding of York West and as my Party's Immigration critic, it is painfully clear that under the Conservative Government one of the greatest frustrations experienced by Canadians is an inability to sponsor relatives from abroad successfully. Not only must they overcome the aggravation of a lengthy processing time, but at the end of that long road all too many applications are rejected. Canadians are asking themselves why. Four reasons help account for that frustration.
First, under the Tory regime the priority for the family class designation has been lowered substantially. Conversely, under Liberal led Governments, family reunification was the cornerstone of the country's immigration policy. In his announcements of the 1987 levels last October, the Minister, who is still not present in the House, limited and froze the family class proportion to only 30 per cent, whereas under Liberal Governments in the mid-seventies and early 1980s the family class stream ranged from an impressive 45 per cent to 55 per cent of the total program.
Second, last June, the Minister refused the Liberal Party's recommendations, contained in the immigration committee's report on family class immigration, that prospective immigrants who have family in Canada should be awarded additional points under the current point system. The result would often make the difference between a negative and positive determination. We also encouraged the Government to expand the definition of "family" so that brothers and sisters of Canadian citizens could also qualify for priority processing. These recommendations were founded on the principles that as Liberals we believe in the important and relevant role played by the institution of the family within the immigration process. For it is the family in Canada that provides the newcomer with a cultural, linguistic and psychological bridge as well as opportunities for employment, shelter and financial assistance. Consequently, having relatives in the country should be elevated to as an important criterion as other variables, such as education, language and job skills. These reforms would be welcomed by Canadians. They would be far reaching toward easing the frustrations that grip many Canadians.
Third, the Conservatives doubled the number of entrepreneur immigrants permitted into Canada. While we all welcome and recognize the economic benefits of business class


Supply
immigrants, this category should not develop into the predominant one and create a situation whereby those immigrants, able to pay their way into the country, would be the only or principal benefactors of our system.
In addition, our immigration officers abroad have reported to me personally that as a result of the ambitious, entrepreneurship targets imposed by Ottawa and the extensive work required to review and approve each single business proposal, financial and personnel resources are being shifted away from the family class sector into the business immigration class. The net effect, of course, of the family reunification applications processed is both fewer and slower. This should not occur. Yet the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) allows the practice to continue unchallenged.
The Minister also refused to increase the visa fees for business immigrants, who are more than able and willing to pay a higher rate, so that additional staff could be hired with the extra revenue to facilitate additional business immigrants. Instead, because the entrepreneur and family class applicant both pay the same $125 charge, imposed for the first time in Canada's history by this Conservative Government, we have the absurd situation where the wealthy are being subsidized by the poor and where the family class reunification is being hampered by the entrepreneurship program. It is a reality which is most unfair and in need of immediate reform.
Fourth, the recent targets for immigration levels announced by the Government are misleading. While the Minister increased the target levels, he has not provided our immigration posts abroad with a proportional increase in visa officers who are required to process the additional immigrants. As a result, in 1986, while the target was established at 115,000, projections indicate that we were going to fall short of that figure by some impressive 30,000 individuals.
Therefore, when the Minister announced a further increase for the 1987 levels to 125,000 without allocating additional resources, he was simply being intellectually dishonest with Canadians because these figures will never be realized. If the Government is unwilling to increase resources to match the increased targets, then it should stop playing politics with immigration targets and honestly inform Canadians of the real number of immigrants arriving and allowed to enter Canada.
When these four factors are taken together, it is obvious why such delay and frustration exists within the family class levels. Again, we call upon the Minister and the Government to re-establish the family class reunification stream as the undeniable, unquestionable cornerstone of our immigration program, and further, that he accepts the Liberal Party's recommendations which would serve to relieve the pressures within the family class system and substantially eliminate the frustrations felt by thousands of Canadians each year when they attempt, unsuccessfully, to have their relatives join them in Canada.
With regard to our responsibilities toward the plight of refugees, and as a signator to the 1951 United Nations
convention relating to the status of refugees and the 1968 protocol, Canada has developed an honourable tradition of humanitarian assistance to those who are displaced, persecuted and who are fleeing in search of a new home. The proud record, Mr. Speaker, for which Canada recently received the Nansen medal took many years to achieve. It was only made possible with the extensive and warm support of all Canadians.
However, the recent actions of the Tory Government are cause for grave concern. In a few short months, Tory initiatives have begun to undo our country's hard-earned reputation in the area of refugee policy. Canadians are witnessing a Government preoccupied with fabricating a refugee immigration crisis and thereby manipulating public opinion in a desperate attempt to bolster its sagging popularity in every part of the country. The Tories are labelling the current situation as a crisis. On this basis they have advanced the regressive changes announced on February 20. The only crisis is the one which lies on the Government benches, the Tories inability to provide moral leadership and compassion in what is one of the most sensitive and emotional areas of federal public policy.
In past years, Liberal Governments, together with all Canadians have demonstrated their belief in a humane and generous refugee program. Canada has welcomed special refugee movements in an addition to annual quotas in response to crises around the globe. Consider the past acceptance in individual years of some 37,000 Hungarians, 12,000 Czechoslovakians, 7,000 Ugandans, 7,000 South Americans, over
50,000	Vietnamese boat people in the late 1970s and early 1980s, 11,000 Lebanese, 9,300 Poles and 3,000 Salvadorans. How shameful it is in the backdrop of these numbers, approved and taken with open acceptance by Canadians, for a Government which now attempts to create a crisis out of some 85 stranded Chilean refugee women and children in Argentina who, with their husbands and families in Montreal, were caught in transit following the changes of February 20, to have refused them entry into this nation just recently. I submit with all due respect that this is a tactic which is morally bankrupt. Whatever happened to the Prime Minister's announcement of August 19 last year when he said in reference to the plight of refugees " ... and if we err, we will always err on the side of compassion, and on the side of justice."
Despite yet another shattered commitment from the Government, I and my Party have faith in the judgment and fairness of Canadians. I have every confidence in their genuine desire to overcome the politics of fear and deception. Together with them, the churches and the countless refugee organizations that have strongly protested the direction of the Government, I call upon the Ministers responsible for immigration to stop turning back the clock on the refugee policy, not to return it to the dark ages but, instead, to present and discuss the straight facts before Canadians and involve them in making the appropriate choices that would be fair, sensitive and just to


those fleeing persecution, and in the best interests of our country and the international community.
Another significant drawback has been Canada's unwillingness to distinguish between a landed immigrant and a refugee. The circumstances moving these two types of individuals to come to Canada are entirely different. While the immigrant seeks to join his or her family, to improve his or her lifestyle and to start anew, something which is completely legitimate, welcomed and acceptable, the legitimate refugee is escaping persecution, torture or death and is seeking a life of order and security. Yet there is one system through the Immigration Appeal Board dealing with the two types of applicants. The result is a backlog and questionable judgments.
As well, an outdated system is addressing a new phenomenon. In the 1960s and the 1970s, the task was largely limited to selecting our quota of refugees from refugee camps around the world. It was then a relatively simple and effective method. In recent years, however, people have been arriving on our shores claiming refugee status and we lack a system capable of addressing them in a fair, humane and expeditious fashion. The backlog is further aggravated and, to a great extent, the Conservative Government is the architect of its own misfortunes. It has failed to act by establishing a new and independent refugee determination system. Such legislation has been promised for the last two and a half years by no less than four different Ministers of Immigration. The Government's inaction cannot continue.
The Plaut report, the Standing Committee on Immigration, the churches, the refugee organizations, the legal community and interested Canadians have all endorsed the concept of a new structure. The Liberal Party's position for a new refugee determination system with proper safeguards and a strong appeal mechanism is crystal clear and was fully explained and illustrated in a recent minority report. Our model advocated a fair and expeditious hearing, one which would discourage potential abuse of and within the system.
The evidence is clearly in, yet the Government continues to stall and to further complicate the system by tinkering with temporary short-term measures. It makes tough policy stands one day only to be followed by intentions of imposing a general amnesty the next day. The Government is adding layer upon layer of confusion and this is causing Canadians to lose confidence in the entire system. In addition, within such a disorderly and unpredictable atmosphere, it is the legitimate refugee who suffers while the chances for fraudulent applications are greatly improved. This situation must stop and it must stop now. We cannot afford further delay. The Government must introduce reforms immediately.
The third failure is the Government's lack of leadership toward developing a long-term strategy for a progressive immigration policy for Canada, a strategy that would seize immigration as a tool to strengthen national unity and create greater economic prosperity. We need a strategy that sensitizes Canadians to the benefits resulting from immigration, a strategy that addresses our nation's massive landscape and
Supply
abundant resources, a strategy that accounts for our dwindling birth rate, our aging population, our need for skilled labour and the net outflow of 50,000 Canadians every single year. We need, therefore, to articulate what role immigration can play and how it can best play that role for the future interest of Canada and its future generations.
Of particular importance is the need to communicate the advantages of immigration and to refute some of the prevailing myths. Throughout the cent' ry, Canada's birth rate has been gradually declining and particularly so since 1960. The fertility rate in 1976 was 1.8 per family. Over the decade, it has fallen to 1.6 as of 1985. Projections indicate that the birth rate will continue to fall to 1.5 by 1991 and to 1.4 by 1996. By the year 2031, our country will begin to face a sharp decline in population. Such a dwindling birth rate has been considered by many policy-makers as being dangerous to a society such as ours with a relatively small population. I would submit that a coherent immigration policy can help to solve that dilemma.
Conversely, Canada has a rapidly aging population. While this can be claimed as being a victory over mortality and ill health, many studies on the age structure see this as being a social crisis for Canada. The ramifications this will have on our labour and employment needs, our social services, our health and educational institutions and our viable continuing support of a pension system are indeed profound and serious. Once again, immigration can help address this challenge facing Canada.
Regrettably, immigration has been perceived as contributing to unemployment. It is felt that immigrants place a heavy burden on the social service infrastructures. Yet study after study has painted a very different picture.
A major 1986 report entitled "The Employment Effects of Immigration: A Balance Sheet Approach" by John Samuel accounted for jobs created by business immigrants, for jobs created by an increased number of consumers, for the skills immigrants have brought with them to Canada and for the capital and investment they have brought into Canada. The study concluded decisively that between 1983 and 1985,
17,000	more jobs were created in Canada than there were immigrants coming to Canada to fill them in those two years. Another report by the same author found that newcomers to Canada generally found employment relatively soon. A 1980 study demonstrated that immigrants spend fewer weeks on unemployment than their domestic cohorts. As well, statistics reveal that of the 10,000 applications for welfare received each month in the Province of Ontario, it is estimated that only 800 originate from refugees.
Immigration can and does increase domestic demand, worker productivity, economic growth and job creation. In addition, there is the value of the skills of immigrants, skills for which Canada has not had to pay. The investment value of the capital and earnings they bring to our shores further stimulates our national economy. The Government, however, has failed miserably to communicate these aspects of immigration and has ignored the solutions an immigration policy can provide to


Supply
some of our more pressing and major social and economic challenges. It is a responsibility that the Government must actively and immediately pursue if it is genuinely concerned about its immigration and refugee policies. I invite the Minister to do exactly that.
The history of this country is deeply rooted in the moving and magnificent saga of a people uprooted by circumstance and history who arrived on our shores to an undying promise of hope and purpose. Make no mistake about it, immigration will continue to play an integral role in shaping the Canada of tomorrow. That tomorrow can, however, be clouded by a Conservative Government which today advances a mean-spirited and disjointed immigration and refugee policy. That attitude and approach must change. It is not in keeping with the proud heritage which the Conservative Government received from previous Governments and Canadians at large.
Future legislation must be of a radically different temperament. It must recognize that social progress and social justice are the fulfilment of freedom. It must recognize that one moral obligation of free men and women and free nations is that of employing all our ability in improving the lot of our fellow human beings. Canada must be a leader in the international community in addressing the plight of refugees. It must not by its actions encourage other countries to opt out of collective international agreements arrived at after many years of struggle and debate. It is also essential for the Conservative Government to remember that this year has been designated the International Year of the Homeless. It must ensure that its philosophy, actions, statements, legislation and leadership is guided by that spirit.
Finally, we in this House and in this country must recognize one undeniable reality. History has placed us all within one common border and under one common law. All of us, from the wealthiest and most powerful to the poorest and weakest share one precious position; we are Canadians. Granted, from time to time it is not easy to remember what that means, but in large measure it means to have left the familiar for the unfamiliar. If the Conservative Government continues to deny the stranger among us, it will be denying the very essence of Canada and its future. I look forward to hearing the Ministers responsible for immigration and government Members as well address this motion today. We should be able to leave this Chamber and use the debate as momentum to indicate Parliament's resolve to create a better country today and a better country tomorrow.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On a question or comment, the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before directing a question to my colleague concerning his remarks, I should like to say where I stand in this debate. If I may, I want to tell the House that my Lithuanian grandmother and my Polish grandfather came to
Canada in 1904. On my father's side however we have been French-speaking Canadians for 200 years. So I might indicate that I am somewhat emotionally divided in this debate, but certain facts did take some significance in the course of my life. This is why I should like to ask my colleague a question about his approach to this issue. He confuses refugee and immigrant, and he refers to the welcoming country which Canada once was and which, as he sees it, is threatened by political changes or quite simply by refugee regulations.
With that in mind I will quote from a February 21, 1987 editorial published in Le Droit and entitled:
So that refugee status might regain its legitimate meaning
-and subtitled:
A pause
In his first paragraph Alain Dexter writes:
A Minister of Immigration in a Government which does not rally full public support has to show some courage to take position on an issue such as refugees. Any decision on so impassioned a topic automatically becomes a controversy.
Mr. Speaker, he goes on to say:
-there exists a commercial trade in human misery.
Were the Ottawa Government to accept unconditionally all foreigners anxious to come to this country it would play into the hands of those unscrupulous "travel agents" who exploit the naivete of people who seek to better their living conditions by looking for a piece of land where prosperity, they are assured, is a sure thing.
And further on:
Some people accuse the Mulroney Government of betraying a long-standing Canadian tradition-
In fact, Ottawa is doing nothing more than reverting to the practice followed by the previous Liberal administration.
So I should like to hear what my colleague has to say, knowing as I do that he is quite sincere. He is the son of an immigrant. I am the granddaughter of immigrants, and 1 should like to have a truly serious response, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I fully appreciate the family history of the Hon. Member for Gatineau. I think she is sincere, as most members are sincere, in relating her family history. However, it was not this Member of Parliament for York West who lumped immigrants and refugees together. What I was attempting to do in the time allotted to me was make the Government aware of the position it is putting immigrants and refugees in when it lumps them together in one stream. We cannot allow the Immigration Appeal Board to judge the immigration application of someone's grandmother from Holland and at the same time deal with refugee applicants from El Salvador. The two are very different. Unless we separate the two, we will not only create a backlog, we will also be making erroneous judgments in life and death matters. It is my duty and the duty of the Government to distinguish between the two and give us a system to deal with them independently. That would be much more fair to both groups and would resolve the frustration many Canadians experience in their attempts to have relatives join them in this country.


The Hon. Member referred to an editorial which suggested that Canada cannot allow everyone from all corners of the world to enter Canada unconditionally. I hope she is not suggesting that I or my Party believe that we can. Everyone knows we cannot accept the 15 million refugees searching for a home around the world. However, what we can do, and what Government has done in the past, is play our role and provide leadership to the international community. If we opted out, as we seem to be doing, given some of the regressive moves introduced by the Government, we will be sending a signal to the Great Britains and Switzerlands of the world that they, too, can opt out. They will use Canada as justification for their actions. If Canada can do it, and it is in the forefront, then we can as well.
The corner-stone of our policy has always been family reunification. That is what Canadians want. That is what they had. My father entered this country with S30 in his pocket. He was able to build a life, educate his children, buy a home, start a small business, and become a proud, loyal and contributing Canadian.
We on this side of the House are suggesting that while we need to take in more business immigrants to help us build a stronger economy, the country will also be built in the future by immigrants who have neither dollars nor investments. Given the opportunity, they will help to enhance and develop this country so that it will become even bigger and better than it is today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his answer, but I would remind him that I also asked a question concerning the editorial sentence which reads:
In fact, Ottawa is doing nothing more than reverting to the practice followed
by the previous Liberal administration.
This is why I am wondering.
What practice?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
It is explained in the editorial. I quote:
the practice ... of having betrayed a long-standing tradition by repealing its
policy under which refugee status claimants were not deported.
It says that the practice existed before, and that it was a practice of the previous Liberal administration. Would Mr. Dexter be wrong?

The Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) should have listened more attentively to my speech. We are not talking about returning to the practice of past Liberal Governments because the phenomenon of refugees has changed. In the 1960s and 1970s Canada played its role by going to the refugee camps and selecting a quota of refugees which would best integrate into this society. That method was very clean, clear and effective. However, in the last several years some refugees have not been waiting for our visa officers
Supply
to visit them in Bangkok, the Philippines or Hong Kong. They are arriving on our shores by sea and by air, sometimes coming across the American border.
The system we used in the 1960s and 1970s was right for that time, but we are now living in the 1980s. We are asking the Government to put in place a system which can meet the needs of the refugees of today. Only then will we be able to build upon the heritage and traditions of yesteryear. If the Member for Gatineau suggests that we should return to the systems of yesteryear, she will be placing her Government in an even more precarious position because that is to say that we should get refugees only from the refugee camps and close our borders. That is not our position.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the Hon. Member for the motion he has introduced. I will have more to say about it later. Would he expand a little on his comments with regard to the Government's recent actions which he finds unfortunate? Would he comment on what he thinks may be the reason for the Government's action? Would he also comment on whether there are similar patterns of action in governments of the United States and western Europe?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the NDP immigration critic for that question. As he well knows, on February 20 the Government moved, in our estimation, in a regressive way. I said that the actions were disturbing and disconcerting because one of the actions was to remove the B-l list from our immigration policy. That was a list of 18 countries developed with Canadians and External Affairs offices abroad. We said that the situations of humanity in those countries were too fierce to deport individuals. Overnight, and apparently without consulting External Affairs, the Government removed those countries from the list and said that individuals from those countries must now apply within the process. The Government has thrown away a number of years of work in producing that list for maximum protection.
When that list was in place individuals from the Soviet Union, as an example, would not be deported and, therefore, were not placed through our refugee stream. By eliminating the list the Government is placing in that refugee determination system thousands of people who otherwise would not have gone through it. Therefore, in addition to it being unfair, the backlog has been increased.
In addition, the Government has touted an agreement which it supposedly has with the United States. To this day we have not seen one line on one piece of paper showing conclusively that there is an agreement between the two Governments. Perhaps in their upcoming meeting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his friend, President Reagan, can elaborate for Canadians on whether such a legal and binding agreement in fact exists. If it does not, they should tell Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think it is unfortunate that today's subject for debate is immigration, since the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) is not in the House and in fact is out of town. I think he would have made a very constructive contribution since, his knowledge of the daily operations of the department, he would have provided the kind of information that I think would have been of interest to Hon. Members on both sides of the House.
In any case, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate, because I believe we all realize the importance of this issue and of the various points raised in the motion presented by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi).
In my opinion, Canada will have many challenges to meet in the years to come, especially with respect to immigration, which has always been, and still is, an important factor of our economic and social life.
The present Government is now giving immigration a new orientation which I believe will better serve the cultural, social and economic interests of the Canadian society.

In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying a few words about future immigration levels. Last November my colleague, the Minister of State for Immigration, announced levels for 1987 of 115,000 to 125,000 new Canadians. This is an increase of 10,000 to 20,000 from 1986. Our reason for increasing immigration levels is fundamental. Canada needs immigrants. We need the growth and enterprise the immigrants represent.
This not an isolated gesture. We have increased the level every year since coming into power. We have sought out new Canadians who can build the economy. We have made room for refugees from camps overseas. We have increased family reunification flows and made the procedures simpler. The Government understands and supports the importance of an immigration policy which emphasizes economic, social and demographic growth.

Mr. Speaker, this Government believes and has always maintained that far from taking away jobs from Canadians, whatever they may be, and I think this is fundamental in this debate, immigrants create jobs. Basically, they bring in capital. They set up businesses. They stimulate consumer spending. No other Government has worked so hard to make Canadians aware of the positive impact of immigration on our economy.
In setting immigration levels, both social factors and humanitarian considerations are taken into account. Family reunification is and will continue to be the cornerstone of the immigration program. We are always extremely diligent in reuniting families separated by vast distances.
Forty-five thousand immigrants in that class will be admitted to Canada in 1987.
In charting this course, we placed unprecedented emphasis on the consultation process. Last year our consultations involved more than 600 groups, including non-governmental immigrant, church and community organizations; provincial and territorial Governments; other federal Departments; and experts in immigration and demography.

Mr. Speaker, we are putting more emphasis on consensus. In December, we sent some important documents to volunteer organizations and the private sector. In those documents we outlined a number of measures aimed at improving the process for consulting with the private sector on immigration levels.
Mr. Speaker, we received many replies, which contained some valid proposals, both regarding the process itself and some specific factors that should be considered in determining future immigration levels.
We fully intend to maintain and refine the practical and compassionate method we are using to set immigration levels in the years to come.

This consultative process has prompted the Government to increase immigration levels over those set by the previous administration. Contrast this with the decline in announced levels from 130,000 in 1982 down to 90,000 in 1984.
With the Government's first level announcement in 1984, we moved to increase immigration in a moderate and controlled manner. Let the numbers speak for themselves. In 1985, we increased the levels from 85,000 to 90,000; in 1986, from
105,000	to 115,000; and 1987, from 115,000 to 125,000. This simply demonstrates our strong commitment to bring more immigrants to this country.

Mr. Speaker, as far as established levels are concerned, we shall not only maintain a humanitarian attitude towards refugees but we will go further. Canada will admit 17,000 refugees in 1987. Of that number, 12,000 will be sponsored by the Government.
Furthermore, Canada is co-operating closely with international organizations dedicated to the cause of refugees, including the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Red Cross, which receive major contributions from this country.
Mr. Speaker, I think Hon. Members are aware that recent events have posed a serious challenge to the Government's refugee policy. The aim of our response has been basically to maintain the credibility of the Canadian government policy. With this in mind, on February 20 we adopted a set of temporary measures-the operative word is indeed temporary-to control arrivals of claimants and to minimize abuse


of the system. We have always said, in the House and elsewhere, that these measures were basically aimed at controlling abuse of the system and thus protecting the bone fide refugee.

Canadians appreciate, even if certain Members of the House choose not to, that these measures to stem the flow of illegal claimants do not signal a move away from the basic humanitarian thrust of Canada's immigration policy. On the contrary, they seek to preserve the integrity of that policy for bona fide refugees. The Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) says that the Government has created confusion and it accuses us of lack of vision.

Mr. Speaker, we are not creating a state of confusion, on the contrary.
Admittedly, the situation is difficult and unprecedented: the facts of immigration have changed and 50 million people in various parts of the world are looking for a land of refuge. This is an international political fact, but not specifically a fact of our immigration policy. Indeed, it is because of the concerns of this Government for genuine refugees that we believed at the time and still believe that the action we took was necessary.
Let us talk about the control measures. While this term might seem frightening and likely to describe a mechanism used to restrict freedom, I believe that some control was necessary. These measures not only show that it is unfair-and I emphasize this basic fact, Mr. Speaker-it is unfair to process the claims of people who ask for refugee status without justification when tens of thousands of people ask to immigrate, and I am indeed talking about immigration, through legal channels, but these measures also indicate that Canada alone cannot solve the problem of international economic disparities.
Mr. Speaker, no government can allow the refugee status process as a subterfuge to allow people to usurp the immigrant status, for which they must basically apply.

Significant reforms are currently before Cabinet and new legislation will soon be introduced in the House reflecting commitment, fairness and efficiency. The Government's record in this regard is indisputable.
In addition to developing this expansionist, enlightened legislation for the future, we have already put in place the most sweeping quality of service changes ever seen in immigration operations. Canadians seeking to bring relatives to Canada can now deal with increasingly streamlined, efficient offices, radically different from the neglected and outmoded standard of service only a few years ago.

Mr. Speaker, most Members of this House are probably aware of the excellent work carried out by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration chaired
Supply
by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), which Committee made 59 recommendations. The importance of providing a quality service to the public, the consolidation of the administrative methods on which officers base their decisions, the acceleration and improvement of the family reunification process for close family members who already have relatives in Canada.

This Government was quick to respond to the recommendations of this all parliamentary committee, adopting more than 50 of its recommendations. Before, a sponsor had to visit a Canada Immigration Centre to sponsor a relative abroad. We are conducting pilot projects on the benefits of doing this by mail. We are actively pursuing other means to ensure that family reunification is dealt with more expeditiously overseas. Decisions will be rendered within months, instead of years, as was too often the case. In order to do this, we will take advantage of modern technologies and eliminate unnecessary steps.

As for processing each claim in the substantial backlog accumulated under the Liberal Government, matters are now progressing well. We are now dealing with the increasing number of claims filed in Canada in an orderly and timely manner. While the number has been high, we have responded to each claim in an orderly and timely fashion.

In short, we have dealt and we continue to deal head on with the variety of immediate immigration issues, as well as with the legacy of neglect inherited from the previous Government. We are also addressing the long-term implications of immigration as no other government has. Although they have come in record numbers, we have responded in a manner that has allowed orderly processing and timely attention to everyone seeking assistance.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member describes the immigration policy as confused. The fact is, and I believe that this is important-
We have to remember that a government must settle a problem with firmness and equity. That the Liberals have never done. I think this is something which could create confusion, but I also think Canadians are fully aware of what we have done and support fully the Government.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians understand our commitment to immigration, to genuine refugees and to our humanitarian traditions. They understand that this Government makes decisions which will benefit Canada, as well as all Canadians


Supply
now and those who will apply for citizenship in the future, both in the short and the long term.
Mr. Speaker, this country has a proud tradition of welcoming people from around the world. We shall maintain and emphasize this tradition in coming years.

We are making the tough decisions both in the long-term and short-term. Let me assure the House that we will continue to make these decisions in the days ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a number of questions. The policies of the Government are certainly tough and they are not humane. They do not, in my estimation, meet with the long-term goals of Canadians, once Canadians are given the straight goods, and the straight goods alone, and they are far from fair to those who legitimately seek entry into this country.
The Minister spent quite a bit of time speaking about increasing the immigration levels and targets. Can he tell the House why, when the Government has increased the target levels, it has not increased the resources to allow our ministries abroad to increase their production, as it were, in order that those numbers can be realized? In 1986 the Minister said the Government was going to allow 115,000 persons into the country, but predictions had only 80,000 to 85,000 people coming into the country. The Minister should answer that question in terms of correlating the resources and the target. The Government can have one million as a target but if it does not attach sufficient visa officers to those posts, it will still be processing 80,000.
The Government talks about family class reunification. Why did the Government's figure of 45,000 only represent 30 per cent of the entire immigration program? In the 1970s and the 1980s it was as high as 55 per cent. Out of those 59 recommendations, I support and compliment the Government on the 50 it approved, but it refused the more far-reaching and implicating type of recommendations, such as increasing the points for people having families here and increasing the definition of family. Why were those recommendations rejected?
Where is the agreement with the United States of February 20? Is it legal? Is it binding or is it a glorified statement between officials of both countries? Why did the Government remove the B-l list without consultations as was specified by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark)?
When is the legislation for a new refugee determination program which was promised going to be introduced? With all due respect, the Minister's predecessor suggested that we would have it immediately after the Plaut report in 1985. The Minister of State (Mr. Crombie) said it would be the fall of 1986. Then it was Christmas of 1986, then January of 1987, this year. Then it was February. We are now in March. Can the Minister tell the House and those groups across the country who are very interested and frustrated with the Government's promises in the last two years, when Canadians
can anticipate new legislation so that the work can really begin?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start with the last question about when the new legislation will be brought forward. It certainly will be done a lot quicker than when the Liberals were in charge. The previous Government took three or four years and came up with only two reports regarding the question of refugees and immigration. I do not believe the Liberals had the courage at that time to face what we face today. They always put off any decision about immigration. They decreased the level of immigration, and that is all they did in 1982. I can tell them that in 1985, 45 per cent of immigrants accepted in Canada are family reunification. We do understand. When I talk about bringing the legislation in pretty soon, I say to my colleague quite frankly that I hope it could be within the next two or three weeks. I say I "hope" because there are many reasons for the delay, the first one being the complexities of this House.
The Hon. Member asks about the agreement with the United States. I know of the Hon. Member's commitment and the commitment of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). I do not want to play the kind of game where we put the refugees at the United States border with more problems than they already have. I can tell the Hon. Member we have all the guarantees. It is not a question of signatures and so on. We have the guarantee, and I challenge my hon. friend to tell me one person who was deported from the United States before requesting the status of the refugee at the Canadian border? It has not happened, and I do not want it to happen. If it does happen, I hope I will be informed by the Hon. Member or by someone else.

Concerning the whole immigration policy, it is my view, following the Hawkes Committee report which was submitted to us by all the people involved, I believe, that actually Canada is asking for just two things: first, that general immigration levels be raised, and, if possible, pretty soon I will strongly recommend to Cabinet that they be raised to 150,000, perhaps
175,000	immigrants a year, and that we be provided with the resources needed to implement that. I am convinced that Canada must not only maintain its immigration levels, but that it definitely must raise them.
As I said, what Canada needs is not just a political formula, I have always said and I will always repeat that Canada was born, developed and enriched by immigration. And Canada can go on doing it. However, this must be done in an orderly fashion and within parameters determined by the Government of Canada, rather than by way of measures that would not respect them.
Again, it is my view that within that process, and I think that the Committee last year proposed-I stand to be corrected if I am wrong-a particular section, a specific part relating to family reunification. I think that is an excellent recommendation. We were not ready at that point to respond, but there


certainly will be recommendations I would think will be made in that direction for the development of our future policy.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, it is my view that the Conservative Government's immigration policy is a consistent one, basically a policy evolving from parameters which respect it.
I will never accept that such a policy be managed on the basis of exceptions. I am just as sensitive as the Hon. Member to the question of refugees, having lived as I have, in the last three months, those events in a very intense way. But as I said, it is my view that this country will not accept that people should, using mechanisms other than those provided by the Act, enter into Canada and take the place of thousands of immigrants who run the risk of not being accepted themselves for lack of being refugees-resort to subterfuge, and take a roundabout way of entering Canada. All refugees, all genuine refugees who apply to Canada will be accepted. Those who are not, and this is a method that has been used far too long already, those who are not will unfortunately have to go through the standard procedure, seeking immigrant status or whatever.

Mr. Speaker, I have two short questions which I would like to ask the Minister. In 1986 the total number of immigrants who entered Canada, including refugees, fell 6,000 short of the Government's minimum target. The minimum target was 105,000, while the maximum was 115,000. The total number of immigrants admitted was 99,000, even though the Government had been warned that the new point system was too restrictive. I want to ask the Minister why the Government did not correct that restriction.
My second question is the following. Nine months ago in its report to the then Minister the standing committee proposed that an information package containing the information needed to complete an application for immigration be given either in Canada to the sponsor of the applicant or to the applicant himself overseas. Thus far little or nothing has been done about those suggestions which would have speeded up the process at no significant cost. In fact, there would have been a saving in terms of time in respect of interviews. I want to ask the Minister why nothing has been done.
Mr. Speaker, will the Hon. Member specify what he means by "restriction" in his first question?

Mr. Speaker, the number of points required was increased from 50 to 70 out of 100, making it nearly impossible for a great many applicants to succeed. Over 180,000 people made the initial inquiry in 1986. Yet we did not even fill the modest number proposed by the Minister's predecessor. That is one restriction.
The other restriction is that the number of points attributable to family relationship was cut from 30 to 15. Therefore applicants were reduced in their ability to meet a standard that
Supply
had been increased by 40 per cent. It is no wonder that the Minister fell short of his target.

Mr. Speaker, this is something about which I would like to look at further in light of the fact that we dealt with a smaller number of immigrants in 1982. The number of people we had on staff at that time was in relation to the number of applicants we had to process. The increased level of immigrant processing does not have to be dealt with with the same efficiencies that were in place at that time. It is possible to improve, and I spoke about that in my speech. We have already improved a great many different parts of the process. I agree with my friend that it has to be possible to improve.
In terms of the main target, we do not want to say that we will accept 120,000 immigrants and accept 100,000. We want to accept 120,000 immigrants. We will consider all the ways by which we can do this. At the same time this is something upon which we can improve. Once again, in 1982, 1983 and 1984 we dealt with 70,000 people. The Hon. Member realizes the complexity of the system. It is not always easy to improve the services and the efficiencies in the great number of offices that we have as quickly as we decide to increase the number of immigrants.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister said that the previous Government put off the question of refugees. Is the Minister aware that in 1982 the Liberal Government admitted three special movements of refugees? It admitted 9,344 Poles following the Solidarity crisis; 3,024 refugees from El Salvador; and 2,501 refugees from Iran. These were all special movements which were taken into consideration in addition to the regular flow of refugees. Just before 1979, with the crisis in Lebanon, some 11,321 Lebanese were admitted. After the Vietnam war in 1975 some 9,060 Vietnamese were admitted into Canada. In terms of Ugandan Asians, in 1973 some 7,069 were admitted. After the Czechoslovakian problem in 1969 some 11,943 Czechs were admitted into Canada. Following the Hungarian crisis in 1957 the Government admitted 37,149 Hungarians. These figures are what led Canada to its receiving the Nansen Medal last year. Why does the Minister not follow the good example that we set in recent years and provide for special movements instead of cancelling them? Why does he not keep up with the record that we established?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that I was not referring to numbers. I was referring to two reports which were tabled during the time the Hon. Member's Government was in power and to one report tabled since we took office. The Hon. Member's Party never had the courage to deal with those two reports. This is not a question of numbers; it is a question of making a very tough decision. The Government of the Hon. Member decided not to deal with the question of refugees but rather to deal with the matter by exception. That is the reality which we face today as a result of his Government. Members of the Opposition want me to deal with the refugee issue by exception. There is always an exception somewhere. Just two weeks ago there was a matter


Supply
involving Chileans, and last week another involving Lebanese. I am sympathetic to the causes, but at the same time we have to be sure that these people are refugees. It is not the Minister who decides if they are refugees or not. It was decided at the time that they were not refugees. The Government of the Hon. Member did not have the courage to deal with changes in refugee and immigration policies. That is what I meant.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend my colleague, the Liberal Party critic for immigration, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), for the introduction of this motion. It provides a good basis for debate. The main point of it is to condemn the state of confusion in which the Government has maintained our immigration policy, particularly the frustration experienced by a large number of Canadians who are unable to sponsor successfully their family members as immigrants and the recent actions which undercut-I would say reverse-Canada's humanitarian assistance and protection for refugees who are legitimately seeking protection in Canada.
First, I want to say that during the debate not only of the last few weeks and months but of the last two or three years I have become aware that there are many men and women of goodwill in all three Parties in the House who are concerned for both immigrants and refugees and who recognize more and more that these are two distinct matters not to be confused with each other. I hope today's debate will contribute to resolving the difficult problems that we have to face. I wish to talk more about the problems than about the possible erroneous attitudes of the Government, even though that subject cannot be entirely set aside. I wish to talk about the history of our immigration policy since World War II.
Second, I wish to talk about the recent attempts which I think will reverse that policy.
Third, I wish to deal with the strong push from Canadians who insist that we not only continue our policy but extend it further and improve it.
Fourth, I want to talk about specific recommendations on that matter. The recommendations which I favour, in line with large bodies of Canadian opinion, are not only my own personal opinion, nor are they the personal opinions of members of our caucus. They were endorsed, if not unanimously then by overwhelming and uncontested vote, at the biannual convention of the NDP a few days ago with the following resolution: "Be it resolved that the NDP strongly condemns the Conservative Government's February 20, 1987 guidelines on the treatment of people who come to Canada to seek protection as refugees; and be it further resolved that the NDP endorses a refugee determination process that is speedy, fair and accessible to all and which ensures the safety of those who seek refuge in Canada".
To develop the first point I mentioned, after World War II Canada greatly increased our immigration policy. In fact, the
population of Canada more than doubled since that time. While it was not all due to refugees-we had the baby boom- we took in many hundreds of thousands of refugees at that time. We developed, as has been said, as the corner-stone of that policy the principle of family reunification. We also brought in independent workers. Many of the manual workers in the factory where I served for 18 years came in at that time. We also brought in skilled workers, although many of them did not get skilled jobs here, and we also brought in immigrants with lots of money. It was one of the criteria used, however informally. I will not go into the political selection that was carried on at that time, which is being documented even now.
The refugees who were mostly selected-and perhaps beginning in the sixties a few were allowed to seek asylum in Canada and to make their claim here-were slowly recognized as a distinct group. Distinct practices, regulations and, eventually, legislation were developed. The United Nations played a vital part in that by developing the principle of asylum, the principle that a refugee is a person with a well-founded fear of persecution for race, nationality, religion, political opinion, or social group. In the five years following World War II, and into the fifties, that criterion was worked out among a large number of the nations of the United Nations, and documents were signed legally, in international law, binding countries including Canada to observe those principles.
Since then, as has been pointed out, Canada has received many thousands and many tens of thousands of refugees, sometimes in large numbers in a short time-and it has done it willingly-from Europe, from Uganda, and from Vietnam.
The rationale for that appears to be that it was in one sense the final stage of the European conquest of North America, doubling the population almost entirely of Europeans in the country. Second, it was also a magnificent source of cheap labour. I remember one of the immigrants in the factory telling me-and he could laugh about it because it was years past-that he was lucky enough when he came over to meet a fellow countryman from his own village who had a construction company and took him to work in his truck every day for a year, until the immigrant learned enough English to find out that he was being paid less than the minimum wage. That happened thousands if not millions of times, and it is still happening.
A third part of the rationale clearly is that we developed a humane principle, the principle that every human being has a right to be protected and that every state in the world-at least every state which signed the UN Declaration as has Canada- has an obligation to ensure that protection, not to close the door and say "go somewhere else".
In the publication Refugees from the UNHCR, the special issue on Asylum in Canada, a very good point was made. It says that it is remarkable "the international community still maintains an agency responsible for the defence of individuals in their relations with states." In other words, the refugee law of the United Nations protects every individual in the world, to


the extent that it makes it a duty of other states, if necessary, to protect an individual against his own Government. It continues:
In 1986 a Group of Governmental Experts' report identified "coerced movements" as sufficiently reflecting the rationale for refugee flight. It is compulsion in a wide sense, including war and armed conflict, which induces flight in fear for life, liberty and security.
They are broadening the definition of "persecution" to fit the facts of our time.
It continues:
UNHCR is a human rights organization in the sense that these basic human values are central to its organizational ethic.
It was very important that we developed that understanding. It would be very unfortunate to have it reversed. That appears to be what may be happening now, and the question is, why?
We have been told that there is a backlash. The Minister himself referred to the backlash in statements at the beginning of January, and he has built on that story which he told us. On January 8-and this was published in Refugees internationally- the Minister said, "we must face up to the reality that two-thirds or three-quarters of the people", meaning the people who come claiming status here, "abuse the system". That is false. The committee, in studying the matter, found that at least 50 per cent of the claimants were in fact either bona fide refugees or had a bona fide claim to humanitarian consideration. In fact, more than half the Chileans, more than half the Salvadorans, and more than half the Guatemalans who applied to our country have been found to be refugees. To slander all of them as being in majority false claimants is in fact promoting the very backlash some people have called racist.
It is very unfortunate that the Government, not just the Minister but senior officials, talked for years about queue jumpers and cheaters as though all refugee claimants were nothing but immigrants trying to get ahead of other people in the line. It is very unfortunate that they have encouraged, whatever their intention was, such a backlash. In fact, two years ago Canadian officials took a leading part in demanding that the countries of western Europe should collude with each other to shut the doors to refugee claimants. Canada's action in the United Nations High Commission Executive was to demand a "get tough" policy with refugee claimants. That is a disgrace to Canada.
We must recognize that our humanitarian policies going beyond the strict definition of refugee were dictated by what Canadians felt was good reason that a person should not be forced to return to the U.S.S.R.; after the Khomeini revolution or coup, a person should not be forced to return to Iran; by the same token, during the period of martial law against Solidar-nosc people should not be forced to return to Poland; and, likewise, people should not be forced to return to El Salvador.
We have had no assurance from the Government that in any of those countries, or in any of the others on the list of 18, the situation has changed so that it is safe to force people to return
Supply
there. In other words, the policy which the Government is now following is a policy of saying: "We will accept refugees only by selection overseas, only if they measure up to our needs for immigrants, whether it is for manual labour, mental labour, or any other purpose". We will not take refugees, is the Government's clear intention, except when we find they serve our purpose. They are to be kept at a distance, thousands of miles, until we give the signal to accept them.
A very foul example of this kind of misleading propaganda against refugees is to be found in The Saturday Star for March 21, 1987. On the front page is an article written by Gordon Barthos. He went to Salvador to find out why Salvadoran refugees were coming. His opening statement is that last year Salvadoran refugees cost Canadian taxpayers $11 million. He begins right away to attack them simply for being here. Then he asks why. He goes on to suggest that the first cause is the earthquake. That is so patently false because, although the big flow of Salvadorans started almost at the very same time as the earthquake, they were coming from the United States, not from Salvador. I am sure the reporter knows that and I am sure his editors know it. It gets worse, Mr. Speaker. He goes on to say:
Before rattled Salvadorans had time to recover from Wednesday's tremor, rebels raced through the city spraying machine-gun fire at several political targets.
In a half page story this so-called news reporter has not one word of acknowledgement of the billions of dollars which the United States has spent to arm and supervise the military of El Salvador in its war against the Salvadoran people by its intensive bombing of civilian villages and the assassinations by government-sponsored death squads. There is not one word in this whole misleading article. Then Mr. Barthos talks about the trickle of Salvadoran political refugees turning into a torrent. Six thousand people is a torrent when we took nearly
100,000	refugees from Vietnam? Mr. Barthos is trying to mislead the public. He goes on to write:
Canadian officials in Central America say deported Salvadorans face no risk of persecution in returning.
That is false, Mr. Speaker. If the reporter had examined the report done by the American Civil Liberties Union, he would know that there are documented cases of murdered returned refugees and that other reports show it to be very difficult to find most of the returned refugees when people go looking for them. They may be there, but nobody knows, and nobody knows what has happened to them.
Mr. Barthos comes close to the truth without actually hitting it when he says:
The war since 1980 has left 60,000 dead and a million displaced;-
He ignores, of course, universally attested statement that it is primarily the Government that has killed those people. The article goes on that the war has:
-caused $2 billion damage to the economy;-


Supply
He says people are forced to work for $4 a day wages. He implies that because, and only because, they are forced to work for $4 a day wages and that therefore they are coming to Canada as economic migrants and not as genuine refugees. His whole article denies the truth of persecution in El Salvador. This is the same paper which, with crocodile tears, published an editorial last Wednesday saying we should help the refugees.
The majority of Canadians have no use for such false propaganda. The Canadian Council of Churches representing the major denominations of the Protestant religion in Canada have called for a program in which the refugee claimant would arrive at the border and immediately be sent for an appointment with the refugee board. He would have a hearing at the refugee board with counsel if he wished. There would be a quick review of any negative decisions, not another hearing, and the individual would have a chance to add any further information. The whole thing would be done in about three months. The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops have said:
We wish to join with other community organizations and church groups in expressing shock and deep concern following the adoption of restrictive refugee measures, as recently announced by the Minister of Immigration.
That was written on February 25, 1987, speaking about the Minister's action on February 20. They say that the Government of Canada:
-must fulfill its commitments and grant asylum to all refugees, as defined by the terms of the Geneva Convention.
The Canadian Jewish Congress has taken the same stand endorsing what they call the "Hawkes model" which provides for universal access and a right to a review on the merits of all cases.
The CSN-
[ Translation]
The CSN said on February 27, 1987.
The right of asylum must be recognized, respected and protected. If persecuted people in this world are to have a way of escaping such situations, the right to seek refuge must actually exist. Any open policy is subject to abuse-it is incumbent upon us to find an effective procedure to discourage and fight such abuse. We therefore request:
(1)	that the right of asylum be fully maintained;
(2)	that the centres for applying for refugee status be maintained, and that the staff concerned be increased.
And, item 8
(8) that the CSN make representations to the federal Government for the repeal of the three measures recently adopted that change refugee access to Canada.

The Canadian Labour Congress has demanded that the Government re-establish the B-l list and that it take measures to speed up the determination process and guarantee that claimants will not be returned to Guatemala or El Salvador. It has demanded that the Government take special measures to ensure Chileans are not unduly singled out as they were by name in the Government's regulation for transit. It was
specifically directed against Chileans. The Congress goes on that the Government should reverse the policy of staff cutbacks in the federal Public Service. In other words, to allow that the good work be done. It wants the Government to ensure that funds are made available to those provinces which are faced with large numbers of refugee claimants so that humanitarian and legal needs of these persons can be met without an unfair drain on provincial resources.
The Canadian Auto Workers write:
We call on the Canadian Government to rescind recent measures directed against refugees. We further call on the Government to resist the temptation to play to one of Canada's most unpleasant galleries: the nativist Canadian element including Government Members, who arouse public passions in spite of their own immigrant roots.
There are many other groups who have endorsed this position. I want to speak about what it means to them. They represent millions of people. First, they want a society based on a commitment to mutual obligations rather than on force or on the advantage of money. Founded on that, they want solid human rights recognized, such as the right of asylum with no turning away from the person in need. What they have said in effect is that what we deny to others we implicitly deny to ourselves. What we wish for ourselves, we must extend to others.
Finally, this calls for a fair division of the labour and wealth of this world. Instead of using those people in El Salvador to run factories for Canada or the U.S. at $4 a day wages and insisting they stay there and work, with their union leaders shot, their co-op leaders shot, their church leaders shot, such as Archbishop Romero, for starvation wages for our benefit, we have to seek a fair division of the world's wealth and work so that those people will stay in the country they love and be able to live there, work there and be our neighbors.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment to make. I was very surprised and indeed shocked that this motion should be introduced today in view of the fact that the number of immigrants admitted to Canada since 1984 has been greatly in excess of the number admitted in the previous two years. This has been a pro-immigration Government which has recognized how immigration has been part of the Canadian story and has a positive contribution to make to the life of Canada.
As I understand it, the Government is attempting not to close off immigration or to reduce it, not to close off our borders to legitimate refugees, but to have a rational immigration policy that gives a fair chance to all who are legitimately seeking admission to Canada. I find that the changes in the regulations affecting immigration have received the most strenuous support from members of ethnic minorities in my own community.
I regret very much the reference to something called nativism. I believe that the support for the Government's policy is nowhere stronger than among the ethnic minorities


who have been outraged that so many people waiting their turn, going through the legal process to gain admission to this country, have apparently found others getting ahead of them in the line. I believe that it remains part of the commitment of the Government that every legitimate refugee who is truly fleeing from persecution will still find asylum in Canada and the refuge that has been part of the Canadian tradition.

Mr. Speaker, I note that the Hon. Member did not ask a question. Perhaps that is because he knew the answer. I am sure the Hon. Member will recognize the following statement if he has read this month's issue of the Canadian Churchman:
"We are of the opinion that Canadians want a policy in relation to refugees that is generous, but just,"-
This comes after the article indicates that "the current government policy is unjust, unworkable and unconstitutional". The article goes on:
"We need a better process," he said. "Immigration officials are not the appropriate people to decide if a person who claims to be a refugee is, in fact, one.
The article goes on:
"The days when we go off to refugee camps to select people to be admitted are over," he said. "The new situation is that refugees will arrive on our shores and at our airports. That phenomenon will not disappear and the government must enact procedures to deal with it."
I hope the Hon. Member is in communion with that sense.

Mr. Speaker, I was curious to hear from my hon. friend about the union movement. In my speech, I indicated that one of the myths that has been allowed to continue is that somehow immigrants increase unemployment and take away jobs from native Canadians. I also indicated that studies clearly show that not only do immigrants not take away jobs but they create them; a general impetus of a healthy national economy.
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) could share with me the viewpoints of union leaders across Canada who are affiliated very closely with his Party. Perhaps he could tell the House about their thinking on the economic equation as it relates to our policy of immigration and refugees vis-avis employment opportunities and the needs that exist within the labour market at present.

Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to report to the Hon. Member that the position of the Canadian Labour Congress for some years has been to redouble our efforts for family reunification and for refugees. The Congress recognizes problems that have been associated with immigration in the past including those to which I and the Hon. Member referred. The mistreatment of immigration workers has the effect also of weakening the position of earlier immigrants and Canadian-born workers. In other words, the congress is wary of how immigrants are used to cut wages or to create unsafe working conditions because of their desperate need. Nevertheless, it has
said that we should redouble our efforts for family reunification and for the refugees.
I do not know if the Hon. Member was listening, but I quoted strong statements from the CSN, the Canadian Labour Congress and Canadian auto workers. I also could have referred to strong statements from the Toronto Labour Council and the Ontario Federation of Labour but I did not have the time to do so in 20 minutes. The labour movement strongly supports a generous refugee policy and a generous family reunification policy.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend my colleague for the very enlightened approach he took in his speech. He pointed out the falsehoods in the story in The Saturday Star and he said that Canadians have no use for that kind of false propaganda. Earlier he referred to a false statement made by the Minister who had claimed that up to two-thirds of the refugee claimants were bogus and then detailed the fact that that was a false statement. Does the Hon. Member have any idea why the Minister would make a statement like that when the facts are completely different? Does the Minister not know the facts? If he does know the facts, why does he not come clean? Why does he try to present a false picture?

Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning, in this debate there are men and women of good will from all Parties. I recognize that only a few months ago the Minister took responsibility for the portfolio of immigration as well as employment. Therefore, he is at the mercy of senior officials who give him their select information and their views. These are the officials who went to a meeting in Geneva in October 1984, the minutes of which record that "the Canadian delegation called upon the High Commissioner of refugees to undertake to study the issue of irregular migration of refugees in its broadest aspects, focusing on identifying the flows, both the source and the destination, the question of fraudulent documentation and associated issues". In other words, Canadian immigration officials have been campaigning for several years to restrict the entry of refugees into Canada. They have not been ashamed to use the newspapers as outlets for their misleading propaganda. I regret that they may have had some effect on the Minister, considering the tremendous responsibilities he undertook last year when he took on the super-large portfolio of Employment and Immigration.
