subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX ON POTATO CHIP INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his recent Budget piled more and more hidden taxes on low and middle-income families. In addition, the Budget imposed a 12 per cent tax on potato chips.
I recently received a copy of a letter that the Manager of the Prince Edward Island Potato Chip Co-operative wrote to the Minister. The Manager wrote, "The P.E.I. Potato Chip Cooperative was founded in May, 1986, and expects to start commercial production in two weeks time." He told the Minister the 12 per cent tax is causing them immense concern. It threatens the survival of their project which otherwise has the potential to make a genuine economic contribution to their region and our province. He also told the Minister the tax will have a very damaging effect on both their business and other enterprises. I ask the Minister to take immediate action to ensure that this industry is not destroyed by his tax grab.

subtopic: SEVENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF 4-H MOVEMENT-SUGGESTED ISSUANCE OF COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
SEVENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF 4-H MOVEMENT-SUGGESTED ISSUANCE OF COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1988 the 4-H movement in Canada and Manitoba will be 75 years old. This organization got its start in the late 1800s in the U.S. Its goal was to improve farming methods by teaching young people new farming skills. Since then its role has expanded to helping youth between the ages of eight and 19 improve their people skills.
Through numerous projects, whether it be caring for a calf and preparing it for show, or participating in public speaking competitions, 4-H members learn co-operation, responsibility and leadership. Lately 4-H clubs have also taken on the important role of educating the public about the continuing importance of agriculture to the economy and the need for support for family farms.
A Manitoba group has requested that a commemorative stamp be issued in honour of this upcoming anniversary. As 4-H has made such a positive contribution to some three million young Canadians, I wholeheartedly endorse this request and urge Canada Post to issue that stamp at the appropriate time.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-CLOSURE OF UNION FUNDED ACTION CENTRES
UNEMPLOYMENT IN BRITISH COLUMBIA-CLOSURE OF UNION FUNDED ACTION CENTRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 210,000 British Columbians suffer the tragic effects of unemployment because neither the federal nor provincial Government has had the imagination or the commitment to adopt a full employment policy. Five years ago the B.C. Federation of Labour tried to help those workers by opening unemployed action centres throughout the province. They spent over $7 million to maintain them. Since the Conservative Government withdrew its funding in 1985 the B.C. labour movement has spent $36,000 a month to keep those centres open. Unfortunately, they can no longer afford the funding and most of the centres will close March 31. However, the problems and suffering continue.
Is it not time that the Conservative and Social Credit Governments took their responsibility seriously and acted to create jobs for British Columbians?

subtopic: DESCHENES COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS-SUPPORT FOR GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
DESCHENES COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS-SUPPORT FOR GOVERNMENT RESPONSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's response to the report of the Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals is indeed welcome news to members of Canada's Baltic, Ukrainian, and Jewish communities. The Government found the problem of war criminals in Canada to be far less serious than originally considered, but that if even one individual guilty of war crimes has sought refuge from justice here in Canada, it is a matter of grave concern.
Canada will try any war criminals under Canadian laws, any investigation would take place under the jurisdiction of the RCMP and the Department of Justice, and we would not create a special organizational body. The findings and recommendations of the commission are fair and just and provide an excellent basis for our Government to develop a Canadian policy on war criminals. I commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for his prompt actions in responding to this report and helping to finally put to rest a most difficult issue.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE JUST AND EQUITABLE LEGISLATION ON BEHALF OF ELDERLY WORKERS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE JUST AND EQUITABLE LEGISLATION ON BEHALF OF ELDERLY WORKERS
speechtext:
Yesterday in Montreal, Mr. Speaker, more than 1,000 early retirees attended an information meeting organized by the Coalition de la defense des droits des preretraites, and they unanimously decided to continue fighting against the injustice which the Government is trying to do to elderly workers.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give only one example. An elderly worker who was earning $385 a week and is eligible for unemployment benefits of $231 but gets a $300 pension from his former employer forfeits any entitlement to UIC benefits. However, another elderly worker who earns $385 a week and is eligible for $231 in unemployment benefits and who gets $300 a week under a registered retirement savings plan is entitled to the full $231 weekly unemployment insurance payment.
Mr. Speaker, I do hope that Conservative Members will continue to pressure their Government so that the Minister will introduce just and equitable legislation concerning all elderly workers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, for years many Canadians living in Canada's north have been treated unfairly. Those who worked for the Government or large companies generally received subsidized housing and/or special wage supplements to compensate for the high cost of living in the north. Those who worked for smaller businesses or were self-employed did not. The Government moved to return fairness to the rest of northern Canadians by making much needed changes to the Tax Act to allow the same benefits through the Northern Tax Benefits Program. I applaud those changes.
Unfortunately, the present eligibility criteria have created tension between neighbouring communities in the Peace country. Unless the eligibility boundaries are adjusted, neighbours in my constituency will be pitted against each other with one having an advantage over the other. I urge the Government to re-examine these criteria as soon as possible.

subtopic: HARASSMENT OF WOMAN FIREFIGHTER AT REGINA AIRPORT
HARASSMENT OF WOMAN FIREFIGHTER AT REGINA AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those on the government side who have recently boasted about the bright future being built for women in this country obviously have not heard about the case of Bobbi Stadnyk. Ms. Stadnyk was one of Canada's few female Transport Canada firefighters and worked at Regina Airport until being fired in 1985. Her case is a horror of harassment and discrimination at the hands of some other staff and management.
In addition to being subjected to lewd behaviour, her equipment was faulty and dangerous and was sometimes tampered with. Her personnel files were falsified, and daily, for a three-week period, insecticide bombs were discharged within the cab of her truck in order to make a dangerous and unpleasant mess for her to clean up. Much of what occurred was with the knowledge, participation, or actions of management.
Three investigations have concluded that Ms. Stadnyk was fired without cause and that she was a victim of harassment. I call upon the Government to do the proper thing, to compensate Ms. Stadnyk fully and offer her another position in the Public Service. The Government must also hire additional airport firefighters whom we so desperately need, and ensure that equal opportunities for those positions are given to women.
* V *

subtopic: DEPARTMENT STORES' CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
DEPARTMENT STORES' CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, news reports claim that banks are reviewing their credit card rates and are expected to cut them before the end of next week. We are also told that major department stores are reviewing their charge card rates. Since those rates are still
28.8	per cent, the level at which they were when the bank rate was over 21 per cent, that review is as late as spring this year is early.
In 1974 when the bank rate was 8.75 per cent the stores charged only 21 per cent. Now that the bank rate is down to 7.14 per cent, what justifies these big stores insisting on a whopping 28.8 per cent? May their review be as short as the patience of their customers has been long.

subtopic: DISAPPROVAL OF LEGISLATION AMENDING PATENT ACT
DISAPPROVAL OF LEGISLATION AMENDING PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by forcing Bill C-22 through Parliament the Conservative Government has proposed to destroy a vital part of Canada's health care system. For more than 15 years Canada benefited from some of the lowest drug costs in the world while still allowing the pharmaceutical companies to be one of the most profitable sectors in all manufacturing industries.
Canadians have expressed their disapproval of this legislation. Thousands have signed petitions, and hundreds of groups and individuals wanted to appear before the Committee on Bill C-22 to voice their concerns about the legislation. However, the Government of Canada and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) have chosen to ignore these concerns. Rather, they are more prepared to listen to the demands of American multinationals and surrender, all in the hope that this might enhance the opportunity for some kind of free trade agreement.
Canadians are not prepared to pay hundreds of millions of dollars more each year in order for the Government to satisfy the demand of foreign lobbyists. The sick and the elderly and the poor should not be made to pay the price for the Government's mistakes. I call on the Minister to withdraw this legislation immediately and to end this unfair attack on the poor, the sick, and the elderly.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the centralization shown by the socialists during their latest national convention is a telling commentary on their Party's democratic discipline. It amounts to centralization with respect to both ideological principles and geography. British Columbia had twice as many delegates as the Province of Quebec. These "twice as many" travelled 3,000 miles to go to Montreal. Quebec socialists who live close by accounted for only 5 per cent of delegates, while Quebecers make up 27 per cent of the entire population of Canada.
The socialists used Quebec as a camping grounds whence the leader tried to kill the old resolutions and define the substance of the new resolutions of his Party. Quebec is not a camping grounds, not for the 1,391 socialist delegates any more than for their leader's camping trailer every year in the month of July.
My advice to the socialists: Study our country. Quebec is a lot more than a camping grounds.

subtopic: CENTRAL AMERICA-CALL FOR END TO UNITED STATES MILITARY INVOLVEMENT
CENTRAL AMERICA-CALL FOR END TO UNITED STATES MILITARY INVOLVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week the leaders of the Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic, and United Churches of Canada urged the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to press for an end to U.S. military involvement in Central America when the Prime Minister meets with United States President Ronald Reagan next month. We in the New Democratic Party strongly endorse that call.
The church leaders have reminded all of us that the U.S. administration's aid to the Contras and its economic blockade of Nicaragua are unacceptable to Canadians.
They have reminded us as well that the continuing militarization of Central America is creating a mounting economic and refugee toll.
At a time when the United States has announced major new military activities in Honduras, involving 50,000 troops, it is crucially important that the Prime Minister put Central America on his agenda and make Canada's voice heard for peace and the withdrawal of all foreign troops and advisers from Central America.

subtopic: CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) brought in his unfair legislation, judging that pensions and severance pay were to be considered as income for the purpose of unemployment insurance, not only did he attack in a discriminatory fashion those people who have retired on company pensions, he also attacked those who are hurt when companies close down.
Consider the situation of Otis Elevator in Hamilton. The Government of Ontario, in an attempt to redress the damage done by the federal Government, brought in new legislation to permit workers to collect severance pay. As a result of the new legislation of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, that severance pay right will no longer be available to those workers.
I call on the Minister in particular to consider the case of the more than 200 workers at Otis Elevator in Hamilton who have a right to the severance pay. They in fact want to continue to work and would have liked to work, except that the company has closed down. They should get support through severance pay benefits.


I plead with the Minister not to bring in this legislation retroactively to cover those workers who have already been forced to leave companies, and to make sure that Otis Elevator workers are included in those who are still able to get severance benefits.

Mr. Speaker, last week a number of us were visited by students who are very concerned about the continuing plight of Jews in the Soviet Union. The facts presented to me by Steven Cohen and Joel Busner, of Montreal, stand in stark contradiction to Premier Gorbachev's much publicized campaign of glasnost, or openness. The students point to the grim statistics which show a drastic reduction in the number of Jews being permitted to leave the U.S.S.R., coupled with continued suppression of Jewish culture, and with the Soviet police practising antiSemitism in many forms.
I know that at every appropriate occasion Canadian Ministers and officials urge the Kremlin to adopt a more compassionate approach toward Soviet Jewry, because our Government does know of the Soviet Union's failure to comply with its international human rights obligations. There are small, encouraging signs toward reunification of a few families with their relatives in Canada.
But the Canadian Government must step up its contact with the Soviets, in the name of religiously persecuted Jews in that country, if glasnost is to mean more than just another word in the Soviet dictionary.

subtopic: TAXATION OF NORTHERN BENEFITS-CALL FOR AMENDMENT
TAXATION OF NORTHERN BENEFITS-CALL FOR AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier in the period for Statements by Members, the Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) rose to complain about the way the Government brought in the taxation of northern benefits. The member is quite correct. About a year ago we knew that there would be a change in the taxation of northern benefits. We tried to get the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to meet with labour representatives and people in the north so we would not end up with the type of system we have at the present time.
The Conservative Member for Peace River is quite right in saying that the system is unfair at this time. However, the Conservatives had the choice. They had the option to meet
with northerners and to meet with the unions affected. They could have brought in a fairer system. It is ironic that the Conservative Government brought down the regulations about which the Conservative Member is now complaining after this House recessed, after we had passed the tax law, and therefore, Members of Parliament were not able to stand in the House and complain about the unfairness before it became a fact.
I call upon the Government to listen to its own back-benchers and to the people in the north, and change the law.

subtopic: CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HELSINKI-CALL FOR RETENTION
CANADIAN EMBASSY IN HELSINKI-CALL FOR RETENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Finnish population in Canada have made a vital contribution to the economic, social, and cultural fabric of this country ever since the first Finns arrived on the shores of Vancouver Island in the mid-1880s. The skills, enthusiasm, and initiative they have shown in building this great nation of ours are recognized and respected by historians and the Canadian population alike.
Today there are well over 50,000 Finns living in Canada making a positive, multifaceted contribution to the Canadian way of life. In light of this important contribution I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to act swiftly to ensure that the Canadian Embassy in Helsinki remains open. In addition, the Government of Canada must continue in its efforts to enhance its historically strong commitment to the country of Finland and to the Finns settled across this vast nation of ours.

subtopic: VISIT OF PRIME MINISTER'S PRINCIPAL SECRETARY TO QUEBEC CONSERVATIVES
VISIT OF PRIME MINISTER'S PRINCIPAL SECRETARY TO QUEBEC CONSERVATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the weekend, Quebec Conservatives were visited by "Royalty"! In fact, Canadians were astonished when the Prime Minister's Principal Secretary, Mr. Bernard Roy, stood up to make a partisan speech before a group of Conservative Members and militants from Quebec. As if this were not enough, the same Mr. Roy decided, unless the Prime Minister made the decision for him, to go before the people of Canada by appearing on the CTV public affairs program, Canada A.M.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the Conservatives are in deep trouble and that in their desperation they are ready to do just


Oral Questions
about anything-in fact the dissent proves it-but there is a limit, even for Conservatives. If Mr. Roy wants to get into politics, let him run for office, and if he wants to be an organizer, he should get himself hired by the Party, but if he wants to keep his present job, I would advise him to stop abusing his office.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Since we started negotiations with the Americans almost two years ago on free trade, we have had nothing but a series of trade harassments emanating from that country. The latest was a decision yesterday by the International Trade Commission of that Government to approve unanimously an application of injury by the $600 million potash industry, particularly founded in western Canada.
On March 3 the Secretary of State for External Affairs said he would personally undertake to talk to Secretary of State George Shultz concerning the potash dispute. Did he raise the matter with Mr. Shultz and did Mr. Shultz give him a commitment that the United States Government would totally and completely disavow the continuing trade harassment in this very important potash case?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I told the House of Commons I would raise this matter with Mr. Shultz and I did so. The Hon. Member would know, because he is not entirely ignorant of these things, that what we have is a pro forma process, a pro forma decision, the first step in a process seeking an antidumping investigation. We certainly intend to do everything we can to ensure that Canadian interests are well protected, but the Hon. Member should not raise false alarms too early.

Well, we received exactly the same kind of assurances in the softwood lumber case which was totally fumbled and bumbled by this Government to the point it is going to cost the Canadian industry $600 million.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade is participating in a meeting with other Ministers of Trade to advance the cause of multilateral trade negotiations. A little while ago some spokesmen of the Liberal Party were in favour of multilateral trade negotiations. I understand from the question posed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry that they are now divided on that, too. They are divided on the negotiations with the United States. They are divided on the MTN. They are divided on the Cruise. They are divided on the question of a nuclear freeze. Is there anything on which they are united?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Secretary of State I would say, yes, we are totally united in standing up for the interests of Canada against those types of trade harassments, something that this Government is clearly not against since every time it gets a chance it surrenders those interests.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA PRESENT CASE UNDER GATT
REQUEST THAT CANADA PRESENT CASE UNDER GATT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the Secretary of State for External Affairs is so interested in multilateral initiatives will he tell us if the Government has now exercised its proper right to go to the international trade forum, GATT, and bring a case against the Americans on potash, basing it on the fact that they are committing a major action of trade harassment?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA PRESENT CASE UNDER GATT

That is a system which grew up under Liberal Governments. As I understand the several positions of the Liberal Party, it seems more or less to want to support the present system in which we are vulnerable to American actions on potash-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM BY AIRCRAFT-POSSIBLE USE OF CANADIAN AIRSPACE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Yesterday the Minister said that the Government has the authority under the International Civil Aviation Convention to forbid overflights of Canada by planes carrying highly dangerous plutonium to Japan. Why is the Government waiting until the United States and Japan sign and ratify an agreement on these flights before taking a stand? Why will the Minister not say right now that, no matter what agreement is ratified, the Government will say no to any such overflights of dangerous plutonium to Japan by the United States?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He knows that yesterday in the United States the International Trade Commission ruled that Canadian potash mines are injuring American producers in New Mexico, a ruling which effectively penalizes Canadians for having more efficient mines and more efficient ore. In light of the statement made by Pierre Gosselin, the Canadian Trade Commissioner in Washington, that the industry will fight this to the end, I want to know whether or not the Government will join in that fight. Could the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the House in detail what steps the Government will take to make the Canadian potash case to American officials?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I understand that after the Chernobyl disaster extensive testing of Canadian caribou and the lichen on which they feed took place and has now been completed. Can the Minister tell us what levels of radioactivity were found and whether the caribou remain fit to eat?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR REACTOR EXPLOSION-TESTING OF CANADIAN CARIBOU FOR RADIOACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to indicate to the Hon. Member and all Canadians living north of 60 and in northern Quebec who use caribou as part of their food cycle that the testing which we did indicated that levels of radioactivity relating to the Chernobyl accident were substantially below the levels in the 1960s when atmospheric nuclear weapons testing was taking place. We will continue to test, but I can tell northern Canadians, as we have through a press release dated, I believe, March 19, that they need not change their dietary habits. All testing we have done indicates that they are not in any danger. We will continue to monitor any radiation on an ongoing basis.

Mr. Speaker, I seek your advice as to whether this should be called a question of privilege or a point of order. I am concerned about remarks made by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary yesterday. I do not wish to reopen a discussion on the substance of the debate, but as reported on page 4429 of Hansard he said: "-when they present petitions-", that is referring to members of the New Democratic Party, "-certified by other Members in a deliberate attempt to create the impression-" and so on. On page 4430 he said:
Privilege-Mr. Heap
-the delaying of the presentation of petitions in order to pretend that a longstanding issue exists is a cheap political trick. It is a complete fabrication and a charade. It is an attempt to mislead the House and the Canadian public.
Further on he says:
-is also a cheap political trick, a complete fabrication and charade, and an attempt to mislead the House and the Canadian public.
Those comments, taken together with those at the bottom of page 4429 and at the top of page 4430 where he said it more indirectly, at which point you warned him, comprise a very clear accusation which is unparliamentary. I request that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary withdraw those remarks.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that you interrupted me, as indicated in Hansard at page 4430, and said that you had heard my words very carefully and indicated that I used the word "if' indicate that you were following the exchange very closely. None of my hon. colleagues in the New Democratic Party sought to interfere with the debate which was going on.
I stand by what I said. I suggested that the effort to mislead the Canadian people into thinking that there was a grand swell of public opinion by distributing petitions to others to distribute was a charade, a complete and absolute fabrication and charade. I was shocked that other colleagues in the New Democratic Party would participate in that charade. Quite frankly, I thought better of them.
As I indicated yesterday, there is more to the petitioning process than coming into the House and handing petitions to colleagues for presentation. I stand very strongly behind the petitioning process. The request for redress of a grievance is very valid, but to come into the House and deliberately put petitions that were certified the day before to four other colleagues is nothing more than a charade and fabrication.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to contribute to the substance of this debate, but I think that some Members of the House sometimes say things which go a lot further than they intended. I know the Parliamentary Secretary to be an honest man. I also know that our rules prohibit the use of the terms he employed yesterday, even if this is done with some ability. I would like to refer to page 4429 of Hansard, where we find the following:
If that is not deliberately misleading the House, it comes as close to deliberately misleading the House as anything in my experience.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member clearly used these words and accused an other Member of misleading the House deliberately. I believe that he should withdraw what he said, to maintain at least some civility in this House. I therefore ask the Hon. Member to think this over and withdraw the words he used if possible.


Privilege-Mr. Heap

Mr. Speaker, I made the request for withdrawal.
I could argue the point and suggest that the precedent claimed by the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary means that we can say anything hypothetically, which has not been a custom in the House in the past, or we can accuse somebody of misleading the House or attempting to mislead the House so long as we leave out the word "deliberately". I believe that this will create a precedent and give the House some difficulties. However, I will not argue the point further.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has raised a matter which gave the Chair some difficulty yesterday. Hon. Members will recall that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary raised a matter which involved the presentation of petitions that had in fact been signed some time before they were presented to the House. His position was that this created an impression that perhaps was not entirely accurate. I believe that is the basic thrust of his comments, which I have deliberately put in very mild language.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said, as reported at page 4430 of Hansard, and has been referred to in interventions today:
If that is not deliberately misleading the House, it comes as close to deliberately misleading the House as anything in my experience.
The Chair is always in the position, when it hears something that may lead to difficulty, that it ought to intervene. Sometimes the Chair intervenes too rapidly and sometimes the Chair waits too long. There is no particular science to it.
In any event, I did rise and say:
I heard very carefully the words of the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary, which were "if that is not deliberately misleading the House", it comes very close to it. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary is also as close to getting out of order as he can be. I will take account of the very careful wording he used, but 1 would ask that he be extremely careful as he continues his remarks.
1 believe I made it clear to Hon. Members at that point that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary was getting awfully close to being out of order. I do not think that should be interpreted to mean, as the Hon. Member for Spadina has warned the Chamber, that just by putting the word "if' in front of provocative words, it will always meet with the satisfaction of the Chair.
The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary went on to say:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I take your admonition.
He continued, and at that point the Parliamentary Secretary was in a close position but nonetheless a proper one. I took it that his remarks were directed not at any particular member of the New Democratic Party but at the New Democratic Party and its particular strategy in the case being debated. After saying that it is a complete fabrication and a charade, the Parliamentary Secretary stated:
It is an attempt to mislead the House and the Canadian public.
Then he went on to say:
The holier than thou New Democratic Party ....
The Chair heard this and was listening carefully. The Chair felt that those words were directed not at any particular member but at the strategy being used by the Party in question.
I will consider the matter carefully, but I must say to the Parliamentary Secretary that I did not take his comments as aimed at a particular member. I see he is indicating that. He may want to make it very clear to the House that my interpretation is in fact correct and that might end the matter, except to say that it is an example of how we must be careful in what we say.
My comments today do not take away from the point the Parliamentary Secretary made yesterday with respect to the use of petitions in the Chamber. I will return to the Chamber at an appropriate time to discuss that matter further. However, if the Parliamentary Secretary would like to indicate to the House that at no time was he directing that particular comment at any particular member, it might be helpful to the Chair.

Mr. Speaker, you have interpreted my intent accurately. I meant to encompass the entire tactics of the New Democratic Party and not to single out any one person as being any more guilty than another. That was my intention.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today which was presented by the Liberal Party condemns the Government for its misguided policy with respect to immigration and refugees. Since my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), who introduced the motion, dealt with the Government's lack of policy with respect to family reunification, I want to concentrate on the refugee question.
First, I want to put this problem into a proper perspective. Hon. Members should know that there is a growing tragedy of refugees and misplaced persons in the world. This has been due in part to the incidence of regional wars, civil conflict and revolutions throughout the world.
Since 1945 there have been 120 regional and local wars in the world, resulting in 19 million deaths. Two-thirds of those 19 million deaths were inflicted on non-military personnel and 16 million of those 19 million deaths took place in the Third World. Those who say we have had peace since 1945 do not know the facts. The figures I just gave the House were as of February, 1986. They are a year out of date. There have been 120 regional and local wars on this planet since 1945 resulting in 19 million deaths. As a result of those conflicts the United Nations estimates there are between 15 million and 20 million refugees in the world today, people who have been displaced from their homes and countries due to conflict, persecution, local wars and so on. The greatest number are from Afghanistan. The next greatest number are the Palestinian refugees. Then there is Iran, East Europe, Central America, Chile and so on.
This human tragedy cannot go unanswered. I would like to remind Canadians that all of us in this country, except our aboriginal people, came here as immigrants or refugees; either ourselves, our parents, our grandparents or our great-grandparents came here after fleeing from conditions of persecution, hunger, or whatever. My own family, which is basically of Irish origin, came here after the famine in 1840 and conditions of persecution.
As Hon. Members know, Canada signed the United Nations Convention on Refugees in 1969, according to which Canada agreed to receive refugees as defined in that treaty, and now as defined in our own law. In order to decide who in fact were refugees under the treaty and who were not, a previous Liberal Government set up a process by which to decide, including a body known as the Refugee Status Advisory Committee.
While this process might have been adequate in the early days of its establishment, it was found in more recent years, with the growing volume of refugees, to not be adequate, that the number of applicants was too great for the system with the result that a large backlog of refugees developed. At one point that backlog amounted to almost 20,000 refugee applicants who had to wait up to two or three years for their cases to be heard by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. This in turn led to more problems in that by the time the applicant finally
Supply
had his case heard after two or three years, he very often had married someone in Canada and had children. It was then extremely difficult to deport him even if it was found he was not really a refugee according to the definition in the international treaty. In other words, the long delay, the backlog and the overwhelming number of persons in the system, led to many problems which led to still further problems.
Faced with that situation, the former Liberal Government appointed the Plaut Commission headed by Rabbi Plaut of Toronto. He was appointed in 1983 to advise on a new refugee determination process and a system to deal with the large backlog. Rabbi Plaut reported back in April, 1985, after a change of Government. He gave his report to the new Conservative Government. That report in turn was referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, of which I am a member. That Committee heard witnesses and heard all points of view and reported to the House of Commons in November and December, 1985.
The Plaut Royal Commission and the standing committee recommended that there be a new refugee determination process which would be quick and fair. It was very important that it be quick, because if it could be decided within two or three months after the refugee lands on our shores whether he or she is a legitimate refugee then that system would discourage fraudulent refugees who come here and get into the backlog, which takes two or three years, knowing that it is difficult to deport them after that period of time.
The Conservative Government of the day responded in part to the reports of the Plaut Royal Commission and the standing committee in May of 1986. The former Minister of State for Immigration promised in May of 1986 that there would be new legislation to deal with refugees in September of 1986, more than six months ago. There was no legislation in September of 1986. There was none in October, November, December, January or February. We are now in the third week of March and we still have no legislation to deal with this important problem.
This morning, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), in answer to a question said that we will see the legislation soon. We have been told that now for many, many months by the Minister and his predecessor and still the legislation is not before us. These delays and procrastination have encouraged more fraudulent claims for refugee status and the problems resulting therefrom have doubled and tripled. Finally, in panic at these developing problems, the Government brought in ad hoc measures on February 20, 1987, which not only shut out the small percentage of fraudulent claimants but also legitimate claimants, those suffering severe hardship, the really legitimate refugees.
In order to support its ad hoc panic measures, the Government is giving a false impression of the refugee situation at our borders. The numbers at our door in recent months have not been greater than those who have come here in special movements over recent years. The special movement which is being denied entry right now is principally from Central

Supply
America and South America. These people are from Guatemala, El Salvador and Chile. The Government said about 5,000 people applied near the end of last year, which has given the perception that that situation is worse than it is. What heightens that perception of something wrong is the fact that we had the Sri Lankan refugees dropped off by boat off the coast of Newfoundland last summer. There was a reverse reaction to that. There was also an adverse reaction to a statement made by one refugee in Montreal who did not like his accommodation in the Lasalle Elotel in Montreal. I think his comments were badly placed. Those comments in that situation received a lot of publicity which was blown out of proportion and gave a bad perception of what is the real tragic situation.
I want to point out that the 5,000 number near the end of last year may sound large, but it is not an unusual number, especially when we recognize that we have between 15 million and 20 million refugees in the world, and considering what we in Canada did in former years. I put that on record to a certain extent this morning in my question to the Minister. I feel it is very important that we recognize what has been done in Canada with respect to refugees over the past few years so that we can see that what we are trying to do now is not extraordinary. In the one year of 1982, in addition to the usual flow of refugees which amounted to 16,900, we took in three special movements. We took in 9,344 Polish people who fled Poland as a result of the Solidarity crisis in that country. In the same year we took in 3,024 refugees in a special movement from El Salvador and 2,500 refugees from Iran. So we took in three special movements in 1982 in addition to the usual flow of refugees. In the years leading up to 1979, as a result of the horrible situation in Lebanon, we took in 11,321 Lebanese. As a result of the end of the war in Viet Nam, prior to 1978, we took in 9,060 Vietnamese and Cambodians. From 1975 to 1979, as a result of the situation in Chile and Argentina, when that country was under a dictatorship, we took in over 7,000 South Americans. At the time of the crisis in Uganda, when the Asians were being expelled, we took in 7,069 Ugandan Asians. In 1969, following the uprising in Czechoslovakia, we took in 11,943 Czechoslovakians. After a similar situation in Hungary in 1957, we took in 37,000 Hungarians. We must recall that at the end of the Second World War when displaced people from central Europe had nowhere to go this country took in up to 186,000 displaced persons per year when the population of our country was but 15 million.
1 have referred to these special movements of refugees, the members of which have all integrated well into Canadian society. They are now leading productive and full lives in this country and have not caused any problems. There are not many of us here in the House who can refer to any of these people as a group which has caused any problems here in Canada. As a matter of fact, we know them as neighbours and as people with whom we work. They are contributing to our society in a positive way.
1 have referred briefly to the refugee movements, which are separate and distinct from the movement of immigrants. We take in refugees, in accordance with a treaty to which I referred, when people are displaced from their countries because of persecution, war and so on. These people are refugees. On the other hand, with respect to immigrants, we set down legislation. We bring in immigrants in accordance with our needs. Last year we brought in 97,474 immigrants. In 1957 we brought in 282,000 immigrants. In 1967 we brought in 222,000. In 1974 we brought in 218,000. During most years in the post-war period we brought in over 100,000 immigrants per year.
When we look back we have to admit that these immigrants and refugees integrated well into our country. They have become good citizens. If there is now a problem with respect to the number of refugees who are at our door it is because the Government has not brought in the legislation which was recommended to it by Rabbi Plaut and by a standing committee of this House. This is legislation which the Government promised to bring in last May, legislation which would have provided for fair and quick treatment of refugees and which would have discouraged false claimants, those who would have jumped the line.
I fully agree with the Government. We have to do something about false claimants, about those who want to jump ahead of others who are in line, but not in the manner in which the Government has undertaken it in its new ad hoc policy announced on February 20. In doing that it not only shuts out false claimants but it shuts out many legitimate refugees. In bringing in this sort of ad hoc policy the Government is playing right into the hands of those in our country who are prejudiced against immigrants. We have to admit that such prejudice still exists today. The Government is contributing to the situation by giving out false information and by leaving a false impression. It may not be doing it intentionally, but that is the result.
In general terms, immigrants contribute much more to this country than they take. They are all consumers. As soon as they arrive here in the country they become consumers. They need homes, clothing, food and household products. They need education and health care. These needs create employment. In addition to being consumers many of them create their own employment by starting small businesses. They pay taxes. In fact, they pay more than their fair share in taxes in many cases because they often have larger families than native-born Canadians. There may be individual cases in which immigrants take jobs which might be open to Canadians. But, on balance, they create more jobs. In any case, our immigration policy over the years, and it is still the case today, was designed to concentrate on immigrants whose skills are needed rather than those which are surplus in Canada. I must continue to make the distinction between immigrants and refugees. As I said earlier, members of refugee movements which we let into Canada in the years since the Second World

War have not caused the disruption that is now being feared by some Canadians.
What are other people saying? We can look to some of the comments in the press with respect to these measures. I have in front of me an editorial taken from the Calgary Herald of February 24, the title of which is: "Restore the refuge". It states:
Immigration Minister Benoit Bouchard has gone overboard with tough measures to curb the wave of bogus refugees flooding Canada.
Rather than being content with addressing the problem of fakes and frauds who want to end-run the system, Bouchard appears to have drawn a bureaucratic paper curtain, nearly as impenetrable as any of iron, around Canada.
I now refer to an article in The Vancouver Sun of February 21, 1987, which is entitled: "Heart and head on the refugees". It states:
The new rules for the admission of refugees to Canada are far from being a perfect way of sorting out the mess created by the lack of a coherent immigration policy. At best they offer an opportunity to stem the flood of refugee claims until the government can finish drafting a new policy that is both humanitarian and practical.
It is distressing that the government is taking so long to produce a program and that it must respond to each new refugee crisis with ad hoc regulations like those announced yesterday by Immigration Minister Benoit Bouchard.
There are reports which we have to the contrary of what was told to us by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). There are reports that some of these people who applied from the United States are being deported from that country. I would now like to refer to an article from The Globe and Mail for February 24, the title of which is: "Refugee claimants may face deportation". It states:
Central Americans awaiting hearings get no guarantees from U.S. officials.
Despite assurances from Canada's two immigration ministers, Central American refugee claimants who are returned to the United States to await an immigration hearing in Canada have no guarantees that they will not be deported.
In Le Devoir for February 23 the policy is described as follows:
-irresponsible and inhumane.

In conclusion, we must do something about false refugee claims. But the Government's ad hoc policy is not the way to go about it. That policy is keeping out many legitimate claimants, as well as fraudulent ones. If the Government had not procrastinated, if it had not dragged its feet, we would not be faced with the specific problems which have led to these misguided measures announced on February 20. Rabbi Plaut and the parliamentary committee recommended a new and improved system in 1985 and 1986-some two years ago. The Government promised action in May of 1986 for September of 1986, and we still have nothing.
I conclude by asking the Minister the following question. Unfortunately, he is not in the House. When will the Government finally act? When will it bring in a Bill that will deal

quickly and fairly with refugees in accordance with our obligations under the United Nations' treaty?

Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions for the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand). First, I wish to congratulate him for having perceived the contribution of not only the skills but the economic contributions that immigrants have made to Canada. He has a great perception of that economic contribution. However, my question concerns the problems we are facing today with economic refugees. Back in 1976, why did the Liberal Government, of which he was a part, not take any measures in respect of refugees who obviously abused the system? Abuses were taking place some 10 years or 20 years ago. I would like to have an answer to that question.
My second question concerns a CBC interview on August 16. I am sorry I could not be present this morning, but I was on the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. However, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) referred to the middle ground as being something like a holding centre, a detainment centre, or what is commonly known as an economic refugee camp. Is this now the policy of the Liberal Party?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is also a member of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, along with me and a few other Members of the House. He has studied the issue along with me. He asked why nothing was done to deal with the problem of refugee abuses in 1976. He is a new Member of the House, having come here in 1984, so I must tell him that there were changes.
Very substantial changes were brought in by the Government in 1981. I believe there were changes in the 1970s as well. I cannot recall the exact year. I have been here 22 years and I have dealt with continual changes to the system.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
I thank the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). In 1975-76 there were changes to the legislation. In 1981 there were changes to the regulations. Also in 1981 the advisory committee on refugee status was set up. Changes were made over the years.
The refugee problem is a difficult one. The Hon. Member will recognize that the problem is becoming more and more severe world-wide. With air travel being what it is today, compared with the early post-war years, it is easier for people to board planes-and for that matter, boats-and leave their countries. Sometimes it the only way they can do it. They do not have time, nor is it safe, to go to the embassy to obtain a visa and so on.
In recent years the problem has become more serious and more tragic. That is why the Minister responsible for immigration in 1983 appointed Rabbi Plaut to come up with a new

system to deal with the problem. The Hon. Member was on the committee with me. We recommended a new system as well. We were more or less unanimous on it. We made a report in November-December, 1985. If the Government acts on that report, I am sure we will have a much improved system, and we will support the Government in bringing in such legislation.

Mr. Speaker, it is curious that the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom) would question Liberal immigration policy when he was quoted recently as favouring only trained workers from western Europe entering the country. Then he tried to hide that by saying it was because they were more adaptable to our winters. I do not think that he should be asking questions about our Liberal policy if that kind of talk is representative of the government benches.
I thought my Liberal colleague articulated very admirably the whole question of refugees. In terms of the question posed by the Hon. Member for Willowdale about why the Liberal Government did not move on some of the things he thought it should have moved on, would the Hon. Member explain something which I think is very important? In the 1960s and in the 1970s the process was to select refugee claimants and our quota of refugees from refugee camps, whereas now, particularly over the last two and a half years to three years, we have been seeing individuals coming to our shores. It is no longer a question of why it was not done in the past. It is more that the system in the past was then and we now have an outdated system to try to address a new phenomenon. Would my colleague be able to make some comments on that particular aspect of the policy?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is correct. In the 1960s and 1970s it was not as common to have refugees simply arriving on our shores and claiming status. That was not the phenomenon at that time. It happened, but it was not as frequently as it happens today. I tried to refer to that in my earlier answer.
I visited Central America and some of the Salvador refugee camps. Even those refugee camps were raided from time to time to time by members of the Salvadoran death squads. Refugees were dragged out of the camps and they were decapitated, only to be found by the side of the road. This sort of thing happened very often because they were opposed to the regime in power. There has been a change in refugee movements and the way in which they have claimed status around the world in recent years.
I did not know of the statement made by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom), but we cannot presume that because people come from western Europe they will adapt more quickly to Canada than people from more southern climates. Some of the most hardy individuals in our winter climate are people who came from South American, Asia, and many other such countries. Many people of our background cannot stand the winter and often go to Florida and the
Caribbean to take in the sun. We cannot generalize on such things.
We have good immigrants and refugees from many parts of the world. That is the way Canada was built. I hope we will continue to live up to the record which earned us that Nansen award from the United Nations last year.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member did not reply to my question on whether he agreed with the Hon. Member for York West that perhaps we should have detention camps in Canada for economic refugees.
The only change made by the Liberal Government from
1981	to 1984 of which I am aware was a consistent reduction of immigration levels every year. Particularly it froze the category of independent immigrants who could make a great contribution to Canada. Why was that done in those days? Today the Government is trying to reverse that whole situation.

Mr. Speaker, I will answer the Hon. Member's last question first by giving him the figures. In 1979 we brought in 112,000 immigrants. In 1980 that figure was increased to 143,000. In 1981 it went down to 128,000. In
1982	it was at 121,000. There was a sharp drop for 1983 and 1984, he is quite correct, but I remind him that we were in a world-wide recession. I do not recall his Party or any other Party in the House suggesting at that time, when the unemployment was almost 12 per cent, that we should bring in large numbers of immigrants. Refugees were always welcome under the law. The point is that in 1983 we brought in 89,000 and in 1984 we brought in 88,000.
Now, three years after the recession, the Government brought in 97,000 last year. It has in no way matched the numbers which we as Liberal Governments brought in during the 1970s and the 1980s. I referred to those numbers earlier. In 1974, we brought in 218,000. In 1967, we brought in
222,000.	Perhaps the Hon. Member could look at the figures over the years. It is true that we dropped in the two years of recession, from 1982-83 to 1983-84. However, I was on that side of the House at the time and there were no questions from Conservative Members asking us to increase those numbers.
When the Hon. Member's Party returns to even the 121,000 figure which we had in 1982, then he can start preaching lessons to us.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Government and also as the Hon. Member for Willowdale, I am pleased to participate in debate on the motion respecting the central role played by family reunification in our approach to immigration.
Our Government has introduced significant and forwardthinking adjustments to both policies and programs as well as to procedures in order to reaffirm and consolidate the priority of family immigration. To suggest otherwise, as outlined in the


motion, is to ignore the numerous important initiatives that have been undertaken. I know, Mr. Speaker, that these adjustments in policies and procedures may not be enough, but in the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, of which I am a member, we continue to work and suggest further improvements, and we expect to meet this week to that end.
The Government's policy regarding family reunification intake is really quite simple. Applications from close family members from abroad which are accompanied by sponsorship undertakings by their eligible relatives in Canada are accepted. It is that straightforward. The only requirements are that the applicants be in good health and of good character, requirements which apply to all immigrants to Canada. For 1987, the planning estimate is 45,000 family class landings. If more than that number of 45,000 eligible applicants come forward, they will be admitted.
By way of clarifying the Government's position in this matter, 1 can only stress that there is no numerical limit on family class immigration whatever. The 45,000 planning figure announced by the Government last November is just that, an estimate of client demand made for administrative purposes. It is not a quota, it is not a ceiling and it is not a target. I think it is important to emphasize as well that the total family class landings in 1987 and beyond will not be affected by increases or decreases in any other immigrant categories. In fact, far from restricting family class levels, we are pursuing measures to expand the scope of family reunification as suggested by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration in reports tabled in this House.
In 1986 our Government introduced a policy aimed at increasing immigration levels in a moderate and controlled manner. It is important to understand that although no restrictions are placed on family class immigrants, there is nonetheless a casual relationship between the global announced level for all classes of immigrants and the number of family class immigrants who are admitted. Simply stated, increased numbers of immigrants generate increased applications for family reunification over time.
For instance, in the past year, the Government has extended eligibility for 119 new occupational groups of selected workers who may be admitted without pre-arranged employment in Canada. This increase in selected worker landings will be reflected in increased family class landings in 1987 and beyond as recently arrived selected workers become established in Canada and begin sponsoring close family members who are still abroad. This will reverse a trend that developed in previous administrations from 1982 to 1985 because of restrictions on independent immigration, and I am sure that my hon. colleagues will appreciate these increases. As I pointed out earlier in the House, the past Liberal administration decreased immigration levels from 1981 to 1984. Our Conservative Government has increased levels since taking power in September, 1984. It is our policy to continue that.

In addition, refugee and humanitarian intakes have also risen in the past three years and many of these immigrants, once firmly established, will also sponsor close relatives who were not able to come to Canada with them. When we combine these developments with the improvements in procedures and processing times, which I will address later, we are clearly looking at a growth scenario as far as family class levels are concerned. In these terms, it becomes clear that the level of family class immigration revolves on sponsorship demand which, in turn, Mr. Speaker, hinges on global immigration levels. At the same time, however, parliamentarians should recognize that there is an element of family immigration that is largely hidden.
It is worth noting that in the first 10 months of 1986, in addition to the 34,239 family class landings, there were an additional 21,420 landings of the spouses and other dependants of applicants in other immigrant categories. The total of 55,659 family members represents fully 70 per cent of all landings in that period. In fact, all successful principal applicants from any immigrant category may be accompanied to Canada by their spouses and dependants. Clearly immigration to Canada is a family movement.
An overview of client and sponsor patterns reveals some other facts that confirm the family's pervasive influence on practically every aspect of immigration activity. During the 1980s, for instance, only 20 per cent of landings can be attributed to the arrival of immigrant children under the age of 15. In 1986, more than 45 per cent of the applicants in the new occupations, opened for the selected worker category, had one or more relatives already in Canada. Some of these applicants will have gained bonus selection points on the strength of undertakings of support submitted by these relatives. This overlapping, interrelated aspect of immigration categories was not lost on the Hawkes committee members. In an attempt to clarify and consolidate the interface between families and the Department, its report recommended the creation of a new assisted family class category constituted of parents with dependants, siblings and non-dependent children.
The proposed assisted family class, and several other closely related recommendations, have far-reaching implications for future immigration policy in Canada. These recommendations speak of a fundamental reshaping of family class immigration that must be carefully considered, both in terms of its effect on operational procedures and its impact on the provinces and private sector immigration organizations.
We have begun discussions on these proposals as part of the ongoing process of consultation that provides the essential input needed to keep immigration policies and systems in touch with evolving needs. Last year, our consultations on the assisted family class and many other issues involved more than 600 groups, including non-governmental organizations; provincial and territorial Governments; other federal Departments; and academics and experts in immigration and demography.

1 want to assure all Members, Mr. Speaker, of the Government's commitment to family reunification as we embark on an era of progressive, expansionist immigration policy. It is widely recognized that for Canada to realize the objectives of this new era of heightened emphasis on immigration, our immigration services must be streamlined. The fact that processing improvements are being implemented both at home and abroad has special relevance to family reunification. Now, family class applicants and sponsors alike will be the beneficiaries of fully co-ordinated procedures more attuned than ever before to their related needs.
While many of these initiatives will be internally generated, the invaluable contribution of the report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration on family reunification must be recognized.
Under the chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) the committee made 59 recommendations that addressed three key areas: the importance of high quality service to the public; the strengthening of the management systems that guide officers in their work; and the acceleration and the improvement of the reunification process for close relative members abroad with their relatives in Canada. The Hawkes report and the Government's fast and positive response to it clearly signalled a long-term commitment to the family unit as the central fact of immigration policy. Already the Government is moving to implement recommendations to expedite the processing of spouses and dependants. The improvements being implemented signify the beginning of a new era for sponsors and their relatives. It is an era that will be characterized by service that is faster, fairer, more courteous and more humane.
What do these improvements mean to our constituents? It will be more convenient for sponsors of family-class immigrants to file sponsorship applications. Families will be encouraged and will find it easier to complete their own applications. The waiting period for sponsorship appointments will be, and in fact already is, considerably reduced. In addition, services for immigrants overseas will be enhanced through more efficient security and background checks as well as through improved medical processing.
These improvements will be an encouragement to all Canadians who want to bring close family members to Canada. They are also consistent with our goal to provide the highest quality of service possible. The way in which we respond to immigrants says much about Canada as a whole and the national values we espouse.
In conclusion, I would reiterate that the one value that remains a constant is the pre-eminence of the family in Canadian life. Immigrant families have provided the very foundation of Canadian nation-building. As we begin to chart an exciting future of increased immigration as an essential element of demographic, social and economic growth, the
family unit will remain the corner-stone of Canadian immigration policy. In Willowdale, there is already some evidence of that. However, some people from the U.S.S.R. are not being allowed exit visas for family reunification in Canada. We have to do a bit more work and apply some more pressure there.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my colleague from Toronto, the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom). My riding of York West happens to be a very multicultural riding, and many people who live there are still in the process of sponsoring their relatives. In my experience, the greatest frustration experienced by those individuals and individuals across Canada is their inability to sponsor relatives from abroad successfully. The Hon. Member for Willowdale has said that the Government is entering into a new era of progress and expansion in family class immigration, but that is hard to believe after looking at the facts of the matter.
In the last immigration targets, the Minister froze family class immigrants to 30 per cent of the entire immigration program. In the mid-1970s and early 1980s, that figure ranged from 45 per cent to 55 per cent. It is hard to understand how the Hon. Member can say on behalf of the Government that we are entering into a new era of progress.
As well, the Hon. Member mentioned that over the last couple of years, the Minister has increased the targets. However, the Hon. Member has failed to inform the House that while the Minister has increased the targets, there has not been the increased allocation of resources needed to process the increased targets. The Hon. Member and I were both fortunate enough to be able to travel with the Standing Committee on Immigration. He as well as I received information from visa officers abroad indicating that it is very easy for a Minister to increase targets, but if he does not allocate personnel and financial resources to meet those ambitious targets, he will simply not get the people coming into Canada. The year 1986 was a perfect example of that. The Minister announced a target of 115,000, but we fell 30,000 short of that. Is it any wonder that we are seeing the frustration of Canadians who are unable to sponsor family relatives from abroad successfully?
I believe it is incumbent upon the Hon. Member to explain why the Minister is playing the politics of targets. If the Government is not prepared to increase resources, then let us not get into an intellectually dishonest campaign. Let us tell Canadians how many people are actually coming to Canada without pointing to targets which are basically not worth the paper on which they are written unless they are supported by increased resources.
Could the Hon. Member tell us why, at the standing committee of which he is a member, the Minister accepted a good number of technical recommendations but failed to agree to two essential recommendations that were designed to break the bottleneck in family class immigration? The first was our recommendation suggesting that there should be more points allotted to prospective immigrants with family members in


Canada in order to recognize the role of the family in immigration, and the second was the recommendation to expand the family class definition to allow brothers and sisters of Canadians to enjoy some kind of priority in processing. Can the Elon. Member explain why the Minister refused to accept those two recommendations?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has some difficulty with statistics. For example, he said that during the Liberal administration, approximately 45 per cent of total immigration was family reunification. That is simply not true. In 1975, family reunification accounted for 34.1 per cent and in 1980 for 35.6 per cent. It was only when the Conservative Government came to power that family reunification as a part of total immigration increased. As a matter of fact, in 1985, it was already close to 46 per cent and we will continue in that direction.
I can understand the Hon. Member's frustration if he is looking at the wrong figures. Last year he said that we fell
30,000	short in immigration. That is simply not true. That is the tactic members of the Opposition have employed continually in the House. They are misrepresenting facts and figures, and the people in our constituencies simply do not understand the truth if the right figures are not made available to them. I understand that last year, the total number of immigrants came to 97,500. That is a figure I got from officials and it indicates that we did not fall 30,000 short. We did fall short by a few thousand, but we are trying to make up for that this year.
Again, it is simply not true that the Minister did not comply with the recommendations of the standing committee. I think we submitted some 70-odd recommendations and only one was rejected by the Minister. He held six in abeyance and was to report back to us on them at a later date. He approved all the others in one way or another. In fact, he approved well over 50 recommendations. I do not know what more the Minister can do. He is one of the best Ministers we have when it comes to responding to requests of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I welcomed the Hon. Member's comments with respect to the Government's intentions concerning immigration. As the Hon. Member will know as I have discussed this with him before, I feel that my family and I would not be in Canada if we had been faced with the immigration policies, procedures, rules and regulations that exist now. My family came to Canada approximately 100 years ago from Britain. At that time, we had no family here. We would not have qualified as family class immigrants. At that time, we had just gone through bankruptcy proceedings in England. We had no capital and could not have come here as entrepreneurs. At that time, we would not have qualified as refugees seeking refuge in a new land so we could not have come here as refugees. It was an era of great unemployment not only in Britain and in Europe but in Canada. Certainly if the rules and regulations we now face as a result of economic

conditions were in place at that time, my family would never have got here and I would not be here.
It is for those reasons that I welcome the comment of the Hon. Member that the Government intends to take some initiatives to increase the number of people who qualify to come to Canada. I suspect what the Hon. Member is referring to, and what the Government has in mind, still would not allow me to come to Canada today under those conditions, but at the same time I welcome what he had to say.
I look on him as an expert in this area and I would like to ask him if, as far as he is aware, it is the Government's intention to broaden the category of family class immigrants. In that way not only the spouses of landed immigrants or Canadian citizens, under age and dependent children and other relatives in those categories would be allowed into Canada, but other family class immigrants such as working children, brothers and sisters and other relatives would be allowed in as well. Is that what the Government intends and, if so, when can we look forward to something of that sort?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is quite right. In those days there were not that many restrictions because there were quite a few independent immigrants who could quickly come to Canada. Those restrictions were implemented a few years ago and we are trying to open it up again. Personally I think there are not enough immigrants, but we also have to think about the family class and refugees. While I would like to increase it even more, it is coming along very well.
Our committee suggested that we should have a population study, such as that currently being done by the Department of National Health and Welfare. We foresee a population for Canada of about 30 million by the year 2000. That would mean that we need to have 200,000 immigrants every year until that year. Naturally, as the Hon. Member suggested, there would be many more independent immigrants in that category and many more family class immigrants. As a matter of fact, if one includes all the independents and the children in the other groups, we can see how in 1986 we had almost
21.000	landings of other independents. That has grown now to
31,000,	and I admit that these are preliminary figures. That brings the total landings estimate which the Hon. Member referred to earlier to 97,474. We are moving ahead. It is perhaps not fast enough, but we have to consider all opinions and we are doing a lot by seeking opinions.
What should the total number of immigrants be? We hope the standing committee will be involved in that once the study by the Department of National Health and Welfare becomes available. We can then ask questions of Canadians. How big a population do you want Canada to have? Is it 30 million? We know the population, we know the death rate and we know the number of children. Unfortunately, Canadians are having smaller families, so the difference will have to be made up by immigrants. That could well mean a figure of more than
200.000	every year until the year 2000.
