speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with interest to the speech made by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom) and the questions and answers which followed. I recognize the obligation on a government Member to put the best possible light on the policies his Government is following. It is easy to talk about a fairer and faster way of handling immigration applications. That is easy to say, but it is strange when the reality of past years does not coincide. It is easy for the Government to point to an increase in the immigration figure. Of course what those figures are is a nice question. As the Hon. Member said, these are not goals and they are certainly not quotas. They are supposed to be targets, but they are not. Last year there was a significant shortfall in family class immigration, 5,000 under the supposed target. There were
10,000	fewer assisted relatives than had been allowed for by the Department in its planning. Why? Primarily because of the lengthy procedures those people faced. As the Hon. Member recognized in giving the figure of 97,000, which he was able to get thanks to the resources of the Department being made available to him as a government Member, that resulted in the Government's hopes for immigration last year not being met. Will they be met in the coming year? Fine words in this House are not going to do it. Much more is required.
Because of the necessity of developing a policy which will ensure the increase in immigration which various members think is necessary, it is useful to have this sort of debate on an opposition motion to condemn the Government for failures in its immigration policy. It has created confusion and suffered from a lack of leadership and vision. That is seriously undermining the confidence of Canadians in the over-all direction of immigration policy.
I want to say something in general about immigration and explore various aspects of the kinds of immigration to Canada that we enjoy these days. I say "enjoy". I know there are many Canadians who have a very real interest in our immigration policy. Many of them want to see that policy conducted in an expansive and fair way. Many are dissatisfied with the way in which the policy has been applied by the present Government and, to some extent, by preceding Governments. I do not think the Liberal Governments did everything perfectly in this area either.
First, immigrants have played a vital role in the development of this country. We can say quite truthfully that we are all the descendants of immigrants. Even the aboriginal peoples might be prepared to recognize a migration to North America once upon a time. Without arguing that point it is obvious that immigration has brought us a great diversity of human resources, cultures and communities. That is a fact and something we should all appreciate. Certainly with respect to multiculturalism, we have a national policy which asserts that that is a good thing. It allowed us to cultivate the consequences of immigration to this country. We need to assert that because
the Minister suggested in a speech in January that there are those who like to celebrate their homogeneous societies and like to think of themselves as untouched by immigration and its various realities. That statement, which I asked him to withdraw and he did not, might have been allowed to pass until now if it had not been for the fact that he brought in guidelines on refugees at the end of February which suggested that he meant every word of what he said. It suggested that he would be quite happy to exclude from this country certain international realities, the creation, if you will, of refugees in various parts of the world and their desperate search for a sanctuary which these days seems to be available only in Canada.
In considering the question of immigration as my friend, the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), did this morning, we face various attitudes over the years. I do not deny the fact that in labour circles in the past there has sometimes been ambivalence about immigration. That was quite understandable in cases where immigrants could be used in industrial relations against those who were then employed or those who sought to better their livelihoods. Wherever there were such experiences, one can understand people reacting against them. That is surely part of the reason the history of British Columbia was so disfigured by anti-Asian feeling from the late 19th century on into this century. It is necessary to transcend that by ensuring that there is fair treatment in the workplace and that employers do not do that.
At various times the reality of unemployment has led people to see immigrants as competitors and to want them to be excluded from the country. We obviously ultimately need policies that will ensure that we are near full employment which will allow us to look with pleasure to the arrival of people bringing in skills and abilities which can be developed and put to good use to build up the economic potential of the country. In the last 20 years there have been very important and significant developments of that sort.
I submit that to regard immigrants as competitors is misguided. As my friend from Spadina pointed out so well this morning, evidence from various labour organizations shows that it is not a concern these days. We have instead a growing recognition of the need for higher levels of immigration to this country in order to ensure that the Canadian population grows rather than stagnates as a result of the very small families which Canadians have these days, the result of which is that we are not even maintaining our population by natural increase.
There had been a suggestion that we should be aiming at a level of 30 million by the year 2,000. That calls for immigration levels well above the 125,000, or a little more that we have at the moment. If the Government recognizes these needs, we will see movement toward 150,000 or 200,000. That is surely necessary. When we do that surely arguments about people being economic refugees, wanting to come to this country not because there is anything wrong in their homeland but only


because it is good here, would fall by the wayside. We want to recognize that when people have skills and see opportunity they should be encouraged to bring their skills to Canada and seek the opportunity of a good life here. In the process they can only enrich Canada by living here, working here, and maintaining their families here.
Every time I hear someone talking about economic immigration or whatever in this critical sense, it seems to me that there is a hint of that kind of opposition to immigration peeking through. I do not think that should exist in the Canadian mind. It should never be expressed by persons in government or speaking for government. We want to rule that out because Canada is a land of opportunity. We very urgently need persons of ability to come here to improve themselves and build Canada.
I said a few moments ago that in the past 20 years laws have been in operation which have brought to this country persons of high ability. That has been a basic factor in the growing diversity of the Canadian population, the development of a multiracial Canada. In 1967 the laws were changed to remove elements that had been fairly clearly racist in their intent. Instead of maintaining a white Canada we began to build a Canada of ability and merit, if you will. We began to accept immigrants who had the education and ability to contribute to Canada. One may say that is, in a sense, creaming off the population of other parts of the world, but I do not suppose I should make very much of that, any more than I should deny the right of others to complain about economic motivation in bringing people to this country.
The high quality of immigration is worth noting. It has many, many consequences. In the City of Toronto there is a remarkably high percentage of people of Asian origin among university graduates. They certainly comprise a much larger proportion than do other segments of the Canadian population. That is one of the realities in a multicultural Canada. It is one of the realities that drives on the demand for full participation by individuals and communities.
It is this sort of experience that has me celebrating immigration year while recognizing that the opposition motion which we are debating today is appropriate and necessary because there have been shortcomings. All the fine words of one member or another from the government benches cannot deny the fact that the perception in the country is one of a tightening up. Many of us have the perception that the procedures are very lengthy in too many parts of the earth from which people want to immigrate to Canada. As a result, we have the low figures which I have already cited, 5,000 and 10,000 below the figures which were supposed to be the target for immigration to this country.
I was talking earlier today to one of my assistants in my constituency who takes primary responsibility for immigration cases, if you will, which come to my attention. We were exploring the situation which faces us, particularly the reaction which public opinion polls suggest is developing among too many Canadians these days. As she said very truly, the fact
Supply
that many people think that the present system is unfair has a good deal to do with the fact that when they try to work within that system they face so many delays and roadblocks that they become terribly frustrated. When they see those who have managed to circumvent the system by extra-legal means of one sort or another they cannot help but become angry. This means that the limited personnel involved in handling cases and the drawn out procedures which presently prevail are really at the heart of the unhappiness which has developed among many Canadians with regard to our present immigration system.
If we were operating the system fairly, if all of the talk about family reunification were actually being acted upon by the Government, if those who seek to bring relatives to this country were able to do so as they should, they would not become unhappy because a group of Tamils from Sri Lanka who had become anxious about their ability to stay in Europe safe from the civil war that is raging in northern Sri Lanka decided to go to a country where they would be safe, namely, Canada. We would not have reaction against their landing on our shores of the sort that we had last August.
In emphasizing the fact of the inability to achieve family reunification I would like to allude to a couple of cases which my assistant, Judith Foulds, has had to deal with. I, of course, have dealt with the persons as well. We have the case of an East Indian family, a physician and his wife. The wife would like to bring her elderly parents to Canada. There have been some medical problems with her parents. Yet they face the declaration of the Canadian Government that they may be a burden on the medical system of the country and will not be allowed to emigrate here. I submit that this physician is perfectly capable of providing for his in-laws and would surely do so.
Now that these people have applied to come here, they are caught in the system, and the possibility of coming to Canada to visit is excluded because of the rampant suspicions in our system that visitors will turn themselves into immigrants. When relatives die in other parts of the world because of the rigidity of our system and the anxiety that our prized medicare system will suffer a slight burden from people from other parts of the world it is nothing less than a system of institutionalized brutality. It is outrageous. That would not happen if we had any kind of humanity in our refugee policy, overseas development aid policy and our immigration policy generally.
When one examines the visitors' visa applications with which we have had to deal, they underscore the lack of political will in these areas at the top of the Department and some levels down. I must also say that the personnel with whom we deal at the lower levels are excellent in their administration and are humane and sensitive in their undertakings. These include personnel at the Thunder Bay office and the lower levels at the head office here.

That lack of political will in the case of visitors' visas is exemplified in another case of an East Indian family. There was an application for relatives to visit. The husband is employed by Air India and the wife is a teacher in India. However, they were denied visitors' papers at the High Commission because of the obvious distrust that they would try to stay in Canada if they visited. It was appealed all the way to the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). There was no resolution, but there was a hard line attitude taken by the Minister and his officials. Such an attitude is an indication of what is wrong not only with the federal Government but with the administration of immigration and visitors' visa systems of government.
The complaints I received reached their ultimate ridiculous point when I tried to help someone from Poland pay a visit to Canada. He was denied a visitor's visa, but all he wanted to do was come to Canada to sightsee, fish, and have a rest. I do not know what else visitors want. He had no intention of working and it was not obvious that he would want to try to stay here. Yet he was denied his opportunity to visit, which perfectly demonstrates the kind of inhumanity that has crept into the administration of our laws. That is the case, whatever may be the protestations of government Members in the House.
This inhumanity reaches its ultimate point when refugees from various parts of the world are faced with similar drawn out procedures and similar hostility in the administration of the law.
I suggest that for the last 200 years refugees have made a vital contribution to Canadian history. As a matter of fact, the bicultural and bilingual nature of central Canada, certainly in the 1960s, was a result of the initial arrival of United Empire Loyalists who were political refugees from the new United States of America. They were refugees as diverse as Mennon-ites, who came here in the realization that they could have a freer life in Upper Canada than in the United States. They were refugees as diverse as the Six Nations Indians who settled in the Red River Valley.
The United Empire Loyalist migration was fundamental to the development of a Canada and les Canadiens. These English and other settlers of great diversity began to build and continue to build a diverse Canada.
I am of Mennonite origin. There was the Mennonite migration of the 1870s and, more particularly, the 1920 political refugees from Soviet Russia who are very grateful to be in Canada.
Let me suggest that refugees from authoritarian and repressive regimes of the right surely are the most valuable addition we could have in this country. They seek a free society in which they can practise their faith, speak their mind, and lead the kind of open lives that it is not possible to lead in a repressive military dictatorship in Chile, the civil war situation in El Salvador brought on by the desire of a few to maintain their power and the desire of the majority to break free from
it, or the Palestinian situation in the Middle East which has not been resolved in over 40 years.
One can think of the Hungarians who left after the abortive attempt to change the society of their country in the 1950s. There are the East Indians who were forced out of Uganda in the early 1970s. There are the boat people of Vietnam. Surely these are people who had some independence of mind in most cases, if not all, and have sought to maintain their freedoms and speak their minds. Surely they are the kind of people we want.
In conclusion, I plead with the Government to respect the letter and the spirit of this resolution as coming from both opposition Parties. It is expressing our intense desire that in 1987, a year after Canada was awarded the Nansen award for its openness to refugees over the years, we cannot go back and see Parliament adopt principles that are truly unfortunate in the administration of refugee requests. Let us maintain the openness that this society should have and increase the numbers we need in order to build Canada for the 21st century.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to the speeches of government Members in this debate as fine words with nothing in the way of substance behind them. I have concluded, after listening to the Hon. Member for some 20 minutes, that his comments were a lot of fine words and very supportive remarks for immigration, whether it be immigration of refugees or others, but lacking in specifics and substance.
Will he outline specifically what his policy and that of his Party is with respect to immigration? Is his Party's policy with respect to refugees to wipe out the recently introduced rules and regulations and return to the rules and regulations introduced in late February of this year? Is it his policy and that of his Party to wipe out all the rules and regulations relating to refugees altogether, as he seemed to imply in his comments? Is it their policy that those who are able to get out of camps or places in which they were detained and come to this country by hook or by crook are the ones whom we should accept? Should we scrap the system altogether and let anyone arrive who wants to come here? Or should we design a new streamlined system which in some way changes the procedures to speed things up? Perhaps there should be a different quota, an increased quota for refugee claimants. What specifically does the Hon. Member and his Party advocate with respect to refugee immigrants to this country? At the same time, can the Hon. Member tell us what specifically he and his Party advocates with respect to immigration generally? Again, is it to scrap all of the system and have no rules and regulations? Or should there be some rules and regulations which differ from the ones we have now? If that is what he and his Party advocate, does the Hon. Member advocate an increase in the quota? If so, has he some specifics in mind as to how much that should be? Does he advocate a broadening of the definitions of the categories of who should be allowed to come to Canada? If that is what he and his Party are advocating, what specifically should it be?


I think rather than being generally critical of the policies of present and past Governments-and I am certainly not immune to that sort of thing-the time has come to be positive and to tell us what he and his Party stand for, not what they are against.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's last words were a gratuitous shot. If I was anything, it was not negative. I spoke of what we needed to do. I celebrated immigration and refugees. The Hon. Member recognized that himself in suggesting he would like to have some specifics as to what the system actually ought to be. I noticed, incidentally, in his previous question and answer exchange with the Hon. Member for Willowdale that the Hon. Member himself was uttering a critique of the policy by suggesting that if the present system had prevailed at the time his ancestors arrived, they would not have been able to stay in this country. That is itself eloquent enough. He is an able Member of the House. If his ancestry had not been allowed to stay here it would have impoverished Canada somewhat. Surely that is what we are suffering these days.
The Hon. Member has asked a great variety of questions. I would not presume to answer them all, although I can start. The answers clearly need to come from the critic for this area rather than from one of the other members. However, to ask if what we should do is to go back to the system which prevailed before the end of February, is to ask one question which is very easy to answer. That system was so unsatisfactory and had been criticized by so many people. We are not that kind of fools. We have humanity. We want the recommendations which have been made in the area of refugee determination to be overhauled. We have more than enough studies on the matter. I remember that a year ago we finally passed the Bill which provided for an enlargement of the Immigration Appeal Board. That is something which should have been done a year earlier. What we clearly need is a procedure under which refugee determination can be carried out expeditiously. We in our Party are quite pleased to draw on the expertise of those who work with the situation. We are quite pleased to look to the work of the Canadian Council of Churches and those groups which come together under its aegis to consider the question. I could take the time to read their recommendations. There are proposals for a refugee status determination which could be completed in about 14 weeks. If it were necessary to have an appeal to the Federal Court, perhaps that would take up to another 13 weeks. That is an expeditious process, a simplified and humane process. That is the kind of action we in the New Democratic Party look for.
As far as targets of immigration are concerned, I believe I was speaking within the parameters of what the Hon. Member for Spadina, as critic, is developing in putting forward what I regard to be a positive program for immigration to Canada.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) for a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, our Party has many spokesmen and I do not think that I will have an opportunity to speak today. However, I would like to make a comment and ask a question to my colleague. I was listening carefully this morning when the Minister spoke about immigration and the refugee problem.
What my colleagues and myself, and especially our immigration critic, have suggested is that Canada should now show some leadership in this issue at the international level. While I am speaking about the refugee issue, I would like to ask my colleague if he agrees with our suggestion that Canada has not only a mission and a responsibility in this regard, but also a duty to do something more in view of its good reputation throughout the world as the problem has become so prevalent internationally. Is it not time to take the first step and even to call if necessary an international conference of major Western countries to deal with the refugee problem immediately? Would the Hon. Member tell the House what Canada should do to fight against the serious international problem posed by refugees, which everyone realizes will become the major problem of the nineties? The refugee problem will obviously become the major problem of the last decade of this century. Because of our privileged situation in Canada, it is our duty to understand the refugee problem. I would like to ask my colleague if he can tell us what he thinks about this suggestion which we intend to develop and to put forward, probably even in our electoral program.
I thank the Hon. Member for that very good question. I am not sure it is going to be a crisis of the 1990s. It certainly is a crisis already in the 1980s.
A world crisis.

Yes, it is already a world-wide crisis. We have massive movements of persons. Some of these migrations are the result of political difficulties of one sort or another, and those are the ones to which the system is sensitive. I think the Canadian Government should look down the road and recognize challenges and needs and see them as opportunities to play a leading role on the face of this earth. I am pleased to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) taking his seat. I would suggest that we have here not simply a matter of refugee determination, not simply a matter of something which should be provided for within immigration, but we have a challenge to our role as peacemaker, if you will. I have become somewhat involved with difficulties in several parts of the world which generate refugees. It seems to me-

As I was saying a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, in various parts of the world we find political situations which are producing refugees. Some of those situations we may not be able to do anything about. I suppose we can do precious little to change the Government of General Pinochet in Chile. We might be able to have some influence on other parts of the earth. I look to the Government of Canada to do its part in these areas, drawing on our Canadian experience with the federal system in which we have not always been brilliantly successful, yet we have retained a peaceable society. We have managed to absorb dissent. We have managed to overcome even violent dissent in this country. Perhaps that gives us some reason for acting in some of these areas to encourage federal solutions, if you will, perhaps a redrawing of boundaries. I do not mean to dodge the question at all. I recognize the world-wide nature of these difficulties. However, I think there are possibilities of going beyond our national defence-based role in providing peace-making forces to certain areas and trying very actively to deal with the political difficulties and to encourage solutions. If we were to do that then the Canadian people could see our activity here as an indication that we want to enable people who want to stay where they are in the world to remain there and to live in peace and security. On the other hand, those who are not able to stay, or those who do not want to, should be encouraged to come here.
1 think a Canadian initiative through the United Nations which would come to grips with this situation is what is needed. The suggestion I have made is designed to keep the global problem within manageable dimensions. Without such manageable dimensions we cannot end repressive regimes, and wars cannot be brought to their end. From such situations we need to challenge other western countries, if they are to be the prime recipients of refugees. I suppose those are the countries about which we are aware in terms of refugees. I suppose that refugees end up in all parts of the world far from our borders and we are hardly aware of them. However, if they are confined to refugee camps in Thailand and Cambodia or in the Middle East that will never be satisfactory. We need to do something about that situation. A United Nations initiative on the part of the Government would be a splendid step to deal with that.
I thank you for your indulgence for allowing me this extra time, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, in their book entitled None is Too Many which addressed the question of why Canada was closed to the Jews of Europe in the 1930s and 1940s Professors Irving Abella and Harold Troper wrote as follows in their preface:
To the condemned Jews of Auschwitz, Canada had a special meaning. It was the name given to the camp barracks where the food, clothes, gold, diamonds, jewellery and other goods taken from prisoners were stored. It represented life, luxury and salvation; it was a Garden of Eden in Hell; it was also unreachable.
They go on to state that the barracks at Auschwitz symbolized what Canada was to all the Jews of Europe throughout the 1930s and 1940s-a paradise, enormous, wealthy, overflowing and full of life, but out of bounds-a haven totally inaccessible.
You might think that it is perhaps inappropriate to draw a parallel between what Canada's policies were in the 1930s and the 1940s, Mr. Speaker, and what they are today. However, I will defer perhaps to a higher authority than myself, namely, Dr. Rabbi Plaut, who authored the report on Canada's refugee policy which was presented to the Government about two years ago. In an article in The Canadian Jewish News of Thursday, March 12, he states:
We have instituted measures which are effective practically, and defective morally. We have signalled a return to former practice which made Canada all too often inaccessible to those most in need of succor.
Last February 20 will go down in Canadian history as a day of shame, for it is the day that our Government closed its doors to refugees.

It was the day when this Government announced a series of cruel measures that go against the humanitarian tradition established in Canada about 40 years ago. It was on February 20 that the Government erected a barrier, not just on the U.S. border but across the world. From now on, refugees who knock on our door and ask for Canada's protection will get the following answer from the Conservative Government: Do not disturb. Don't call us, we'll call you.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) tells us that our policy is unambiguous, and I quote: We offer asylum to all bona fide refugees arriving in our country.
The Minister does not say that the Government has just erected a barrier around Canada to ensure that no one will be able to enter the country. The Minister does not say either that the true objective of his policy is to discourage refugees from knocking on our door. The Minister does not say that the message transmitted throughout the world is that Canada's doors are now closed.

It has been made abundantly clear in recent weeks that the Minister of Employment and Immigration and a bunch of mean-spirited Tory back-benchers call the shots when it comes


to the Government's immigration policy. The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner), the junior Minister, does not have a word to say about the formulation of policy. But he has become the major apologist for the Government. The Minister of State for Immigration says that real refugees will never be sent back. He says that every claimant will be entitled to a fair and open hearing. Should we believe him? After all, the Minister of State is an honourable man. Let us examine what has happened in the past month.
On a snowy Sunday one week after our Government closed Canada's borders to refugees I visited a refugee shelter in Plattsburg, New York, 60 miles or so from Montreal. I talked to refugees at the shelter who are fleeing violence and death threats in Central America. Many have been living underground in the United States. They were homeless, penniless, scared and, in many cases, separated from their families. They came to our border and asked for Canada's protection. We told them: "Wait for a month or two in Plattsburg and then we will admit you to Canada for an immigration inquiry".
When they were turned back at the Canadian border these people had their first encounters with U.S. immigration authorities. They were forced to sign documents voluntarily agreeing to leave the United States. Many were living underground and had not had any previous contact with U.S. immigration authorities. If not accepted in Canada they will not be allowed to stay in the United States and, presumably, they will have to return to the countries they are fleeing, or face deportation. They were not quite sure what awaited them a month or so down the road in Montreal.

Among those I met, Mr. Speaker, there was a boy with his mother and sister, all three from Guatemala, whose father had been in Montreal for some time. Our Government is obliging them to wait at the border for at least a month, in uncertainty and squalor. Why make them wait? The Government is making them stay at the border pending an inquiry in Montreal that will rule on their application for refugee status, a process that may take several years. During that time, they will be able to stay in Canada. Making them wait at the border, 1 should point out, makes no difference to the investigation. Does it make sense to make them wait 60 miles from Montreal while they could just as well wait for the inquiry with their father in Montreal, and enjoy the support of the churches and various organizations that provide assistance to refugees? Why make them wait? Mr. Speaker, this is harassment. The Government is making them wait for no reason at all, in squalor and uncertainty, at the Canadian border, because the Government and the Minister want to discourage and prevent refugees from entering Canada.
As of February 20, the Government also requires transit visas for refugees from some 98 countries who plan to stop over in Canada en route to another destination. People from
Supply
these 98 countries include refugees who used to be on our nondeportable list. The countries include Afghanistan, El Salvador, Guatemala, Iran, Cambodia, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, and Viet Nam. Just to recite the names of these countries tells us that they are countries torn by violence and war to which our Government, up until now, considered it too dangerous to deport refugees. They are countries, Mr. Speaker, in which neither you nor I would want to live and would think twice about visiting these days.
Refugees from these countries are often lucky to get out with their lives. Now they are told by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to put their lives in further danger by openly presenting themselves to Canadian embassies and consulates and indicating that they want to leave their countries permanently. Does the Minister not understand that going through such bureaucratic procedures is a luxury which refugees cannot afford? Does the Minister not understand that refugees are lucky if they have the time to pack a bag and run?
The Minister says that he wants an orderly process. I can tell him that he has succeeded. Transit visas are indeed very effective, as we can see from the example of the Chileans who were caught up in Argentina. The Minister did not even have the basic decency to allow for the fact that they had already left Chile for Canada at the time the new measures were announced on February 20.
Last August the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) urged Canadians to show compassion toward the Tamil boat people who had arrived on our shores. At the time he said: "It is not the presence of 155 frightened human beings searching for freedom and opportunity that is going to undermine Canada or our immigration policies". Never a finer statement was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but it begs a question. If 155 Tamil boat people will not upset our whole immigration policy, why would a few thousand bus people from Central America over the Christmas holidays upset it?
In recent months the Ministers responsible for immigration have actively promoted the idea that we in Canada are facing a wave or flood of refugees. I note the use of words which convey a sense of natural disaster. However, what evidence is there that we are facing an unmanageable number of refugee claimants?
Last year, 18,000 claims were made in Canada, not more than the number of people it would take to fill an average hockey arena in Canada. The Minister of State for Immigration stated on a number of occasions that because we took in a thousand a week in the first few weeks of 1987, we would have reached some 52,000 by the end of the year. Perhaps that is what he was afraid about. However, is it accurate that this number of refugees would have continued every week throughout 1987?
What evidence is there? The Minister has not given us an iota or scintilla of evidence to prove that his forecasts were anywhere near realistic. Indeed, a recent decision of the United States Supreme Court on the rights of refugees in that


Supply
country will probably have the effect of substantially reducing the numbers that would have come to Canada.
When I was in Plattsburg, representatives of local social service agencies told me that rumours had been circulating for weeks that Canada would bring in tough new refugee rules. If this rumour had reached Plattsburg, is it not logical to assume that the unusually large numbers which we saw in the first few weeks of 1987 were people who were trying to get into Canada under the wire? I would remind the House that in the last few weeks before the Berlin Wall was put up in 1962, thousands of refugees crossed from the East to the West because they knew it would be their last opportunity to do so.
What evidence is there to suggest that Canadian society has reached its capacity to absorb or integrate refugees or immigrants? Have we reached that level? The evidence suggests that we are far from it.
Let us look at what our country was capable of doing for Indo-Chinese boat people. At that time the Government showed leadership. I am happy to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) present in the House today. He was the Prime Minister at the time the Government appealed to the better instincts of Canadians, to the generosity of Canadians, who sent up sponsorship groups in community after community across the country. We opened up our military bases and chartered aircraft. Since 1979 we have taken in over 100,000 Indo-Chinese refugees, with over 60,000 in 1979 and 1980 alone. Today, seven years or eight years later, all these persons are contributing to our country.
The question I would put to the Government today is: Why not act in a similar fashion in 1987? Why not, if we are afraid of a large number of refugees perhaps coming to Canada because of inhumane laws in the United States, remind President Reagan of his responsibilities? Why not call an international conference on Central American refugees where each country would agree to welcome a certain number of refugees? Such a conference was held in 1979 to deal with Indo-Chinese boat people. Why not show this kind of leadership?
Instead, we have a Government which has let the situation deteriorate. It has delayed bringing in legislation to deal with refugees for over two years now. The Government has also failed to commit adequate resources and has taken no action against fraudulent counsellors and travel agents.

In Quebec, some people say our province has taken more than its fair share of refugees. In fact, that was the conclusion of a poll published in Le Devoir a few weeks ago. It is just not true. We have ranked fourth for at least seven or eight years, coming after Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta.
Mr. Speaker, some people insist that immigrants are taking away our jobs. I would like to thank Senator Rizzuto for suggesting the following argument: If it is true that immigrants are taking away our jobs, how come Ontario, which year after year has received three times as many immigrants
and refugees as Quebec, has an unemployment rate of only 6 per cent, while Quebec's unemployment rate is 10.5 or 11 per cent or more?

Canadians are a generous people. If presented with the facts, they will respond positively with generosity. Canadians are capable of rising to the occasion as they did with the IndoChinese boat people.
I have had occasion to work with some of the people who help refugees and immigrants-non-governmental organizations, church groups, and immigrant aid societies. I visited refugee camps in southeast Asia in 1980 at the height of the crisis. People who work with immigrants and refugees are extremely dedicated and committed. If we present them with the challenge, they will respond.
These groups are dismayed with the policies of the Government. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who was here several minutes ago, shook his head when I drew some parallels and said that the doors of our country were closed to refugees. He seemed to disagree. I ask him to speak with the people in the Mennonite Church whom he knows intimately and to ask them what is their opinion of his Government's policies. These groups, Mr. Speaker, will not accept these policies and will not stop fighting until they are changed, until this Government adopts the recommendations of the Plaut report, the report of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and introduces a refugee determination process that is independent, fast and fair. Our Government is capable of better. Canadians are capable of better.
If I might just close my comments on what I regard to be a rather depressing situation, perhaps one can make a point better in a humorous fashion than one can in a serious fashion. A predecessor of mine in the Liberal Party, Sam Jacobs who was the Member of Parliament for Cartier district in the 1930s, which takes in much of the same area that I represent today in the riding of Laurier, once said that Jesus of Nazareth would be barred from Canada under current government policies. Why, Mr. Speaker? There are four reasons? One, he would not have a proper passport. Two, he had no relatives in Canada. Three, he would not be travelling to Canada by a continuous journey-the same thing could be said about the refugees who now require a transit visa. Four, he was a carpenter. Who needs carpenters? Mr. Jacobs also at one point said that the policy of the present Government on immigration is like the wisdom of God, it surpasseth understanding. The same thing could be said today.
I hope that the Government will review its policy introduced last February 20, read history and listen to what people like Rabbi Plaut are saying. Again, I would ask the Minister for National Health and Welfare to speak to his friends in the Mennonite Church and ask them what they think about these policies. He was part of a much more generous Government. I


would ask the Government to show leadership and tear up the shameful refugee policies that were introduced last February 20.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) who I think spoke with compassion and integrity. His interest in the over-all subject of immigration and the plight of refugees goes beyond a one day debate in the House of Commons. The Member has been very active on that front.
I was interested by the debate earlier on with respect to perhaps paying some attention to the international community and to the international obligations that we signed on behalf of the plight of refugees in 1951 as well as the protocol of 1968. If Canada has been a leader-and it has-then the type of policy announcements that we have seen coming down the pipeline will send a very dangerous signal to other countries. We will soon see the Great Britains and the Switzerlands begin to retract, and regrettably they will use Canada as a justification for doing so.
If we are to play that educational role in calling for an international agreement or a strengthening of those agreements through an international conference, what about a domestic international campaign which the Government ought to begin to initiate? It should present Canadians with the straight goods. The Government should begin to put this in the perspective of our declining birthrate, of our aging population, of an outflow of 50,000 Canadians each and every year, of our needs in terms in skills and labour and those jobs that you and I, Mr. Speaker, perhaps do not wish to do as well, as the other benefits we have been talking about. What are the views of the Hon. Member for Laurier in conducting that type of domestic educational campaign and structuring a positive constructive role rather than trying short-term temporary solutions that only feed off misconceptions and fear for the benefits of a political Party?

Mr. Speaker, it would be great for the Government to undertake an educational campaign but it would have to change direction 180 degrees from what it has been doing. We have a Government which is morally bankrupt. It has manipulated public opinion. People are beginning to see through this facade. There have been a number of well-thought opinion articles and editorials in newspapers across the country which point to the hypocrisy of the Minister of Employment and Immigration . . .

-who wept crocodile tears when he heard about the poll published in Le Devoir which said that Quebecers thought they were getting more than their fair share of refugees. This is the same Government and in fact the same Minister who let the system deteriorate for two years and procrastinated and failed to introduce the Bill all groups have been waiting for, the Bill that will correct the present situation.

I agree the Government could set up some kind of policy or campaign to educate the public, but that would require a drastic change from what we have been seeing in the past few months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, primarily I have a comment. As you know, Ministers do not very often intervene in the comment or Question Period. I think it is important for me to comment in view of some of the statements the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) has made which are erroneous-I cannot use an unparliamentary word to describe them. He said that the refugee numbers have decreased. The member used the 1979-1980 figures. He did not mention that it was a Government at that time, along with many volunteers, led by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who initiated that policy together with the present Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald).
Let me come to the present situation. It is not true and it is patently false when the member says that refugees are being cut off by decisions taken by our Government in February. In fact, the number of refugees has increased. The Government made a very clear point when we assumed power that we would increase immigration. Immigration flows when we came into Government were 89,000. The 10 year average is about
140,000.	Most of us who had some dealings with immigration in the past know that we have to increase those numbers. That is a given fact.
We also know that if we look at demographic factors Canada is below replacement value. The demographic studies taking place now in the Department of National Health and Welfare as we look to the turn of the century show that immigration has to increase. Immigration has been good for Canada. Statements should not be made which are not in keeping with the facts.
In 1984 we had 89,000 immigrants. The Government came forward with an amendment, which I moved way back- supported at the time-that the Government of the day had to come before Parliament and give annual targets. We did that. We hoped that we would have an improvement in the economy and there would be new employment, which is taking place, and we said we would increase that figure to 105,000 in our first year and that we would increase it to approximately
125,000	the next year. What other decisions the Government will take when we have to appear before this House-I think it is in November this year-will again show an increase.
Let us look at refugees specifically. We increased the refugee numbers along with the entrepreneurial class. We went to 12,000 of government-sponsored and another 4,000 of cosponsored refugees. Just recently, after the announcements here on the refugee matters, I was in Traiskirchen, the basic camp from which eastern Europeans come. I met with NGOs there. To a person, they told us to keep our refugee policy.


Supply
They said we cannot jeopardize a good policy. We did win the national humanitarian award. There is integrity in the system.
There are convention refugees who cannot come into Canada because of jumping the queue. It is not the Conservative Government that does not want more refugees and it is not the Liberal Party nor the NDP. It has nothing to do with partisanship. It bothers me when there is this twisting of the facts.
We have increased the number of refugees and, I would think, we will increase it again. That is natural in the Canadian context. Hon. Members may put forward their partisan views but I would hope that they would at least put them forward with a factual point of view rather than to score political points based simply on information that is not factual.

Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of respect for the Hon. Minister but I must ask him to get in touch with some of the people he knows in the Mennonite Church and ask them about their position on the Government's current policies. It is not just members of the misguided Opposition who are saying what I have said. I refer to the comments of Rabbi Plaut. He said that we have signalled the return to a former practice which made Canada all too often inaccessible to those most in need of succour. Does the Minister think that Rabbi Plaut is also misguided?
I would point out that I did mention the initiative begun by the Government which was led by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead. That initiative was based on a much sounder moral ground than the one of the current Government. The policy as it related to Indo-Chinese refugees was very humanitarian and was carried through by our Government.
The Hon. Member spoke of refugees that we select at our visa offices abroad. I would point out that we did not fill the number of positions available for those selected abroad last year. Does the Minister think that that kind of procedure is appropriate for all refugees? Does he think that refugees should put their lives in danger in many cases by openly presenting themselves at Canadian offices abroad and indicating that they want to leave their country permanently? Does he think that this is an acceptable risk for many refugees to take?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the Hon. Member. In Mennonite communities, there is the same kind of division of opinion as that expressed by the Hon. Member. My father who is a member of the Mennonite
Central Committee was a refugee who came through that system. Always there was respect for the manner in which one had to address the issues, laws and regulations of the country.
Many people do not understand immigration. Immigration has been good for Canada. However, we cannot leave the impression that those who come here through conventions or by being sponsored by voluntary organizations are not coming here under the laws of Canada. The Hon. Member has asked if people should put their lives in jeopardy. At present, Canada does take people who are not convention refugees and cannot have a hearing. The regulations are quite clear on that.
Let us take a look at the number of refugees. In 1981, the total number of refugees, both convention and otherwise, was 14,996. In 1982, it was 16,908, in 1983 it was 13,643, in 1984 it was 15,400, in 1985 it was 16,550 and in 1986 it was 18,625. The Minister of Immigration has indicated that he is looking at an increase in that number. However, it must be done in a way that does not put immigration as a whole in jeopardy. That is the point we are making, and I think many Canadians agree with that point. That has always been the bottom line for immigration in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Minister, as I have throughout my comments, that under the guise of stemming abuse, the Government has slammed the doors of Canada shut. The Minister talks about the need to respect and address the laws of the country. I suggest that our country has an obligation under international refugee conventions and our Government is not respecting the spirit and the letter of those obligations.
Refugees who would run great risks in presenting themselves at our visa offices abroad will be shut out from any recourse by the policies the Government implemented last February 20. I would ask the Minister to think about the situation in which some people find themselves. There are those who do not have the time to present themselves at a Canadian Embassy abroad and there are those to whom no such embassies are accessible. Some embassies have been closed down by the Government because of the financial straits in which it finds itself from time to time.
Refugees from Lebanon often find that their home towns are bombed flat in the middle of a war. They do not always have the time to line up at a visa office abroad.
Again, I would suggest that under the guise of stemming abuse, the Government's policy has slammed the doors shut on many refugees who really counted on Canada as being one of the last countries in the world to present an open door and a humanitarian attitude. If the Minister is really sincere about wanting to address the problem of refugees, I would suggest that he encourage his colleagues to implement as quickly as possible the recommendations of the Plaut report and the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Immigration. The standing committee recommended that a new refugee determination process be instituted, a process which would be independent, impartial, quick and fair to refugees. Refugees



should be treated in that manner rather than with the kind of cavalier attitude that we have seen from the Government since last February 20.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for .Jonquiere (Mr. Blackburn).

Mr. Speaker, we have reached an exciting and significant moment in the history of Canada's refugee policy, and it is my privilege to speak to that part of the motion that is more specifically concerned with refugee issues. I am looking forward to seeing the development of a progressive policy in this area and to following the progression of that policy very closely with the Members of this House.
The Government's measures with respect to refugees continue to reflect a commitment to humanitarian principles. Canadians can be proud of what this country has achieved in the area of assistance to people who reach our borders after having been victims of oppression and persecution. I am looking forward to a debate on this policy by the Members of this House. Too often, such debates only take place when there is a crisis, and are then quickly forgotten.
The motion before the House today urges the Government to adopt a fair, humane and efficient refugee policy which would reinforce Canada's past proud tradition and honour Canada's international obligations under the Geneva Convention signed in 1951.
As far as our immigration policy is concerned, Mr. Speaker,
I would like to point out that the Nansen Medal was awarded to Canada on November 13 last year in recognition of its tireless commitment to refugees from countries around the world. It is the highest honour awarded by the United National High Commission for Refugees to those involved in assistance to this group.
Mr. Speaker, awarding a prestigious medal to an entire nation is a rare event. That tribute was paid to us as a result of the co-operation and dedication of a great many individuals and organizations. We have every intention of remaining faithful to the commitment for which we, among all other nations, were found worthy of such regognition, and of maintaining our efforts on behalf of immigrants and refugees.
In 1987, for example, Canada will welcome more than
20,000	people under refugee and other humanitarian programs.
This is the kind of generosity which characterizes measures taken by Canada on behalf of refugees and which singled out our country as the deserving recipient of such a great honour.
More measures will be taken with respect to refugees. For instance, participation in the activities of international agencies abroad; settlement assistance for refugees; signing sponsorship contracts; intervention of action groups.
Supply
We agree, Mr. Speaker, the Government does have a role to play but it cannot act alone. Religious groups and nongovernmental organizations can participate actively by helping refugees and immigrants. Sponsorship and initiatives in settlement cases are so important that they are covered under the Immigration Act. Indeed, the whole process began in 1979 at the suggestion of a Conservative.
For all practical purposes, it was the official aim of new cooperation which included consultation, policy drafting and participation in resolving settlement problems, determining required services, and setting immigration levels.
Now, Mr. Speaker, a few words about sponsorship. The refugee program is a model, particularly because of strong sponsorship on the part of private groups. The best example is the Nansen Medal which was awarded to us last November. We now have in excess of 50 sponsorship agreements, proof positive that the Government and private agencies are working together to relieve suffering people.
In 1979-80, 32,000 people came to Canada under the sponsorship of about 7,000 groups encouraged, once again, by the dynamism and initiative of the Conservative Government. Over the past five years, more than 18,000 refugees were sponsored by private groups which helped them get settled in this country. Hon. Members of this House cannot but applaud such worthy efforts.
Let me say a few words, Mr. Speaker, about starting costs. Despite the increasing cost of dealing with the flow of refugees and the costs involved in the adaptation assistance program, we have in no way reduced funding in that area, quite the opposite. Three years ago, $30 million were used as income support for 10,000 Government-sponsored refugees. In 1987, because we are aiming at 12,000 refugees, that amount should go up to $50 million. Those monies have already been earmarked for that purpose.
In addition, this Government does not intend to reduce the amount of assistance offered. We will seek by all means to achieve a better control over adaptation assistance program funds.
Let me now refer to agency funding. We recognize the value of services offered to newcomers by private agencies. We are committed to supporting them. The funds allotted to the immigrant settlement and adaptation program for the coming fiscal year have been increased to $4.9 million.
As far as language training is concerned, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission has launched a pilot project, the newcomers language training program. Immigrant women outside the labour force are an important target group. This is another example of this Government's innovation. We have recognized the need to implement a federal program to meet special language training needs.
Mr. Speaker, the project allows women to get out of language ghettoes and to assume better their rightful place in Canadian society. During the coming months, the Canada


Supply
Employment and Immigration Commission and the Department of the Secretary of State will review their language training programs, with a view to strengthening the Canadian Government's role, and more importantly, to establishing a program that will meet the various needs of people who have just entered Canada.
What about legislative measures for acknowledging refugee status, Mr. Speaker? Our commitment to refugees is as steadfast as ever. It will be strengthened when legislative measures for the recognition of the status of refugee are tabled in the coming weeks. The draft proposals are in their final stages, Mr. Speaker. This is an extremely important and complex matter which requires our undivided attention.
The growing number of claims, which went from 8,400 in 1985 to 18,000 in 1986, should reach 50,000 this year. Mr. Speaker, it is important that Canadians should realize this constant increase. I repeat that the figures-8,400 in 1985;
18,000	in 1986; and probably over 50,000 this year-have forced us to take temporary control measures in order to set up a new process without having to face an overwhelming number of claims.
However, Mr. Speaker, we must make sure that we have a fair and adequate system.
Our legislation will emphasize certain elements. It will make it possible for us to protect refugees while preserving our reputation all over the world as a compassionate country. The legislation will reflect also our moral, legal and international commitments.
The new legislation will reflect the contributions of many groups, including the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, and that of Mr. Plaut.
Particular attention has been paid to the opinions of sponsoring groups and ethnic organizations.
Here are some of the highlights of the proposals announced last May: First, the setting up of a commission of immigrants and refugees independent of Canada Employment and Immigration Board. Second, hearings by an independent tribunal which would give claimants the benefit of the doubt. Third, an impartial climate during the hearings. Fourth, an appeal authorization before the Federal Court of Canada and, fifth, an access which would not jeopardize the integrity of our immigration program.
These elements had to be reassessed in the light of the new events which have occurred since last May, but, as a whole, the characteristics of the new process combining justice and effectiveness, will be maintained.
The new refugee determination process will discourage the abuses which have prevented the process from being effective these last few years, and the Hon. Members know what I mean by that. For instance, we found out that Turkish nationals who
wanted to come to Canada were abusing the process. These abuses were eliminated. We have slowed down the rapidly increasing number of people crossing our borders, without however exposing a single one of them to being sent back to his country of origin. However, Canada will always ensure that genuine refugees have the best protection possible.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian delegate to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees said the following on February 25: Canada was unfortunately the victim of such abuses, and it has unfortunately had to take a number of measures to protect itself. But even so, explained our representative to the High Commissioner for Refugees, the methods used by Canada are much less drastic than those applied by certain other countries to stop an excessive inflow of refugees.
We have to keep up our tradition.
At the international level, Canada has sponsored initiatives to organize to some extent the procedures used by various countries to face the refugee problem and prevent those who already benefit from a certain protection from bypassing the process at the expense of people who really need this assistance, that is people who really need our help. Various international organizations as well as the High Commissioner for Refugees have supported such initiatives, which will very soon have positive results.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add that Canada was built by immigrants and refugees. They met their challenges with pride, integrity and success. We shall continue to be proud of their achievements because they are for us all the guarantee of a brighter future. Indeed, we believe immigration to be increasingly important for the future development of Canada for a variety of reasons. First, there are economic reasons, because we believe that immigrants create more jobs than they take away from the Canadian economy. They take part in the economic growth and development of this country by contributing to the creation of capital, by increasing the demand for Canadian goods and services, by providing needed skills and dynamism to our labour force and by contributing to the tax revenue of all levels of Government.
Also, socially and demographically, I might add that my Government is convinced that immigration is a major force which contributes to the economic and social prosperity of Canada and which has allowed our country to take the lead when international solutions have been needed to solve the problem of refugees and immigrants whose cases involve humanitarian considerations.
